data.agents#Coding agents:
Since v0.7.0 the gateway serves the three APIs coding tools speak, in front of the cluster’s own models. Every request authenticates with a virtual key as the bearer token and goes through the same budgets, guardrails and fair-share priority, so an agent’s consumption lands in its team’s share.
Tool speaks Route Notes OpenAI chat completions POST /v1/chat/completions the default for editors such as VS Code with Continue OpenAI Responses POST /v1/responses stateless only: no previous_response_id, no stored responses Anthropic Messages POST /v1/messages vLLM’s native Anthropic endpoint, no translation in the gateway
data.anthropic#Agents that speak the Anthropi:
POST /v1/messages lets an agent that speaks the Messages API use a local model. The gateway’s README says to point such an agent at the gateway “with a virtual key as the bearer token”. The request shape is the Messages API’s:
curl https://llm.example.org/v1/messages \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $LLMFLOW_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model": "llama-3.3-70b", "max_tokens": 256, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]}' How a given agent is told its base URL and its key is that agent’s own configuration. Claude Code is documented below, from Anthropic’s pages; for any other agent, read its documentation, which this site has not opened.
What the gateway guarantees on this route: guardrails cover system, text and thinking blocks, tool_result content and the strings inside tool_use inputs; guarded streams pass through an Anthropic event filter; error bodies carry "type": "error"; /v1/messages/count_tokens (since v0.12.1) goes to vLLM’s own endpoint and returns an exact count, which Claude Code uses instead of its estimate; it is authenticated and rate limited, not charged and not guarded. Accounting counts cached tokens as vLLM reports them.
data.claude-code#Claude Code:
Everything below is from Anthropic’s pages LLM gateways, connect Claude Code to an LLM gateway, the gateway compatibility guide and legal and compliance, read on 2026-10-26. Claude Code versions change; check them.
Which models, said plainly. Anthropic’s page says it “doesn’t support routing Claude Code to non-Claude models through any gateway”. Pointing Claude Code at this gateway’s /v1/messages and a local vLLM model is technically possible, since the route exists, but it is unsupported by Anthropic. The supported path is Claude models: Claude Code, then this gateway, then the Anthropic API through the opt-in anthropic provider (gateway v0.12.0), billed to the organisation’s own API account.
data.claude-code-anthropic#The supported path:
With v0.12.0 the gateway can send /v1/messages to Anthropic’s API instead of to vLLM. The configuration, with what check-config enforces (an explicit allow-list, allow_external, one API key per institution, and pii and hide_secrets guardrails), is on the Gateway page. For Claude Code it means:
Point ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL at the gateway and use the institution’s llmflow virtual key as the credential (below). The gateway accepts it as Authorization: Bearer or x-api-key, so Claude Code’s ANTHROPIC_API_KEY works too. The gateway replaces it with the organisation’s own Anthropic key; the client’s credential and the OAuth anthropic-beta capability never go out. The traffic is billed to the organisation’s Anthropic API account, per token, in USD, and shown as USD in the gateway’s budgets and reports, apart from GPU-hours. Not a subscription. The gateway never relays a Pro or Max login, and pooling subscriptions is forbidden (see Subscriptions, the legal and DPO notes there, and the gateway’s own statement that this is not legal advice). /v1/messages/count_tokens is routed since gateway v0.12.1, to Anthropic with the organisation’s key; it is not charged, and the same masking applies, since a count also sends the prompt off the site. Prompts leave the site. That is why the guardrails are mandatory, and why the route needs your DPO’s agreement.
data.claude-code-credential#The base URL and:
ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL points Claude Code at the gateway; Claude Code then calls /v1/messages. The credential comes from one of three places, and each sends it in a different header:
Credential Sent as ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN Authorization: Bearer ANTHROPIC_API_KEY x-api-key apiKeyHelper both headers The gateway reads the virtual key as a bearer token (above), so ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN or apiKeyHelper fits it.
Recommended: apiKeyHelper, reading the key from a file of mode 0600, so that the key is never in an environment variable or in a file that is committed. The helper is a command that prints the credential and nothing else (Claude Code caches its output for five minutes by default; CLAUDE_CODE_API_KEY_HELPER_TTL_MS changes that). A one-line script:
#!/bin/bash cat ~/.config/llmflow/key with chmod 600 ~/.config/llmflow/key, referenced from the user settings file, ~/.claude/settings.json (%USERPROFILE%\.claude\settings.json on Windows):
{ "apiKeyHelper": "~/bin/llmflow-key.sh", "env": { "ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL": "https://llm.example.org", "CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC": "1" } } Never put a credential in a project’s .claude/settings.json: it is committed and shared with everyone who clones the repository. A per-project credential file is .claude/settings.local.json, which Claude Code adds to your global gitignore when it saves a setting there; if you create it by hand, add it to your gitignore first.
CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1 keeps background traffic off other hosts (version checks, telemetry, release notes). It also disables auto-updates, so plan another update path.
For the VS Code extension, there are two setups. Anthropic’s pages are connect to an LLM gateway and Claude Code in VS Code.
1. The documented, reliable setup. ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL and the credential go in claudeCode.environmentVariables, in VS Code’s own user settings (the command Preferences: Open User Settings (JSON)). Anthropic says the extension checks credentials from this setting before launching, so it is the reliable place for the credential, and that values in ~/.claude/settings.json reach the spawned process but not the extension’s own login check:
{ "claudeCode.environmentVariables": [ { "name": "ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL", "value": "https://llm.example.org" }, { "name": "ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN", "value": "llmf-..." } ] } This puts the key in VS Code’s settings file as plain text. Keep that file out of any synced or committed location (Settings Sync, a dotfiles repository), and use a key meant for this one purpose, so that it can be revoked on its own.
2. A key file and no key in settings. Not verified. The VS Code page says, for third-party providers, to check Disable Login Prompt (the setting claudeCode.disableLoginPrompt, “skip authentication prompts (for third-party provider setups)”) and to put the provider configuration in ~/.claude/settings.json, which “ensures your settings are shared between the VS Code extension and the CLI”. By analogy, the apiKeyHelper setup above, in ~/.claude/settings.json, with claudeCode.disableLoginPrompt checked, would keep the key in a 0600 file and out of every settings file. This page has not verified it against a gateway, and the connect page’s statement that the extension’s login check reads claudeCode.environmentVariables is what makes it uncertain: try it, and confirm with /status, before relying on it.
Run /status in Claude Code: an Anthropic base URL line, and an apiKeyHelper line naming the credential, confirm that the gateway is in use.
Pinning an organisation to the gateway. Managed settings with allowedProviders: ["customEndpoint"] and the gateway’s ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL in the file’s env block make Claude Code refuse any other destination (Claude Code v2.1.285 or later). CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_GATEWAY_MODEL_DISCOVERY=1 adds the gateway’s models to the /model picker.
data.claude-code-project#Attributing requests:
What each client sends: Claude Code adds x-claude-code-session-id, x-claude-code-agent-id, x-claude-code-prompt-id and x-claude-code-request-class (among others), but nothing that names a project; Continue sends only the headers you configure.
Available from gateway v0.13.0. The gateway reads the project from a header, X-Llmflow-Project by default (the name is attribution { project_header }, and default_project names the project used without the header; see Project attribution). The value is a project name looked up in the key’s own team; a project that does not exist, is disabled, belongs to another team, or is not allowed to the key’s owner gets the same generic 403, “project not allowed for this key”. The role must be stored in the gateway (or come through SCIM): a role that exists only in an SSO token does not count.
The recommended setup keeps the secret and the project apart. The credential is personal, in the user’s settings (apiKeyHelper above). The project is not a secret: it goes in the repository’s committed .claude/settings.json:
{ "env": { "ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS": "X-Llmflow-Project: my-project" } } ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS takes one Name: Value pair per line, with \n between pairs in a JSON string. Anthropic notes that headers like these count as headers that need approval, and that when they come from a project settings file Claude Code applies them under the rules for when it applies env values: the user is asked to approve them.
For Continue, the header is set per model entry, with requestOptions.headers (Continue’s reference):
models: - name: Large model (B300) provider: openai model: large-model apiBase: https://llm.example.org/v1 apiKey: ${{ secrets.B300_GATEWAY_KEY }} requestOptions: headers: X-Llmflow-Project: my-project
data.claude-code-subscriptions#Subscriptions: While a gateway credential or an apiKeyHelper is active, requests carry that credential instead of a claude.ai subscription login, and the subscription’s limits do not apply; the traffic is billed per token to whoever owns the credential the gateway forwards. Pooling Pro or Max subscriptions behind a gateway is not allowed: Anthropic’s legal and compliance page says it does not permit routing requests “through Free, Pro, or Max plan credentials on behalf of their users”, and customers “may not pay for, resell, or intermediate Claude usage on their end users’ behalf”. Read that page, and the consumer terms it cites, before planning any shared use.
data.continue#VS Code with Continue:
Continue is configured for the gateway exactly as for any OpenAI-compatible server; the file and its keys are on the VS Code page, taken from Continue’s own documentation. Point apiBase at the gateway’s /v1 and use the user’s virtual key. Whether a given Continue version can call /v1/responses is a question for Continue’s documentation, which this site has not opened for that route: the safe choice is /v1/chat/completions.
A request through /v1/chat/completions that the gateway accepts, whatever the client:
curl https://llm.example.org/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $LLMFLOW_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model": "llama-3.3-70b", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]}'
data.limits#Limits to keep in mind: A Responses stream under post-call guardrails is refused: ask with "stream": false. A guarded stream that carries tool-call arguments in the chat API is stopped; ask without stream. A client chat_template is stripped, and so are priority, extra_body and the other engine fields. The performance of the current release is not measured yet.
data.responses#The Responses API, and why it:
A client that uses /v1/responses must send the whole conversation in input each time. The gateway forces "store": false and answers 400 to previous_response_id, background, conversation and a stored prompt:
curl https://llm.example.org/v1/responses \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $LLMFLOW_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model": "llama-3.3-70b", "input": "Hello"}' Why. vLLM can keep responses in the memory of the instance that produced them (VLLM_ENABLE_RESPONSES_API_STORE=1), readable and continuable by anyone who holds the id. The gateway forces store: false and refuses the stateful fields regardless, so a deployment with the store enabled stays safe: on a shared cluster no tenant can read or continue another’s conversation. GET /v1/responses/{id} and the cancel route are not routed.

data.alerts#Alerts: Soft-budget alerts are retried with exponential backoff, up to 6 attempts, and every webhook attempt carries the same Idempotency-Key so that a receiver can de-duplicate. Retries live in memory: a gateway stopped mid-retry does not resume.
data.anchors#Anchors: Every checkpoint, and the entries it covers, is also written to the anchor export (audit/checkpoints/.json, audit/entries/-.jsonl.gz). On S3 the objects go under Object Lock retention when the bucket has it enabled; create the bucket that way, since MinIO and Ceph RGW require it at creation, with versioning. A file export refuses to overwrite a file but does not stop its owner. The age of the newest exported checkpoint is the metric llmflow_audit_anchor_age_seconds, and a checkpoint still unexported after anchor_max_lag raises the alert audit_anchor_lag.
data.audit#Audit and logging: v0.5.0 of the gateway (roadmap milestone M3) answers three questions: who changed what in the administration, can that record be trusted, and what may be kept about the requests themselves. This page is written from the gateway’s README at that tag; where the guarantees end is stated as plainly as where they hold.
data.configuration#A configuration:
This was run through llmflow-gateway check-config v0.16.1, with the key files present and a configuration (organisations, a pool and a model) around it.
store { kind = "postgres" dsn_file = "/etc/llmflow/pg.dsn" spool_dir = "/var/lib/llmflow/spool" } audit { signing_key_file = "/etc/llmflow/audit.seed" checkpoint_interval = "5m" anchor = "archive" anchor_max_lag = "15m" retention = { admin = "61320h", auth = "8760h", scim = "8760h", system = "8760h" } prune_interval = "24h" } export "archive" { kind = "s3" endpoint = "https://minio.example.org:9000" bucket = "llmflow-audit" path_style = true access_key_file = "/etc/llmflow/s3.access" secret_key_file = "/etc/llmflow/s3.secret" prefix = "gateway-1/" lock_mode = "COMPLIANCE" retention = "8760h" queue_size = 1024 } logging "research" { teams = ["lab-nlp", "lab-chem"] destination = "archive" content = false max_content_bytes = 1048576 batch_records = 500 batch_interval = "1m" lock = false } policy "attributed" { teams = ["lab-nlp"] require = ["user", "metadata.project"] require_tags = true } policy "long-context" { max_body_bytes = 33554432 max_response_bytes = 134217728 } The signing_key_file is an Ed25519 seed, made with llmflow-gateway audit keygen -o FILE. Like every *_file attribute it may be a vault: reference instead of a path.
data.exports#Export targets: kind is s3 or file. gcs and azure answer “not implemented”. The S3 client is go-volumes/s3. Exports go through a bounded queue; a batch dropped or given up is counted and alerted (export_dropped, export_failed), never silent.
data.log#The admin audit log:
Every state-changing admin request is recorded, accepted or refused: the actor and their roles, the action, the target, the state before and after, the request body, the status, the client address and a request id. Events the gateway raises itself go to the same log: SSO logins and logouts, key rotations, SCIM reconciliation. Key secrets and tokens never appear, and reads are not audited.
The log is append-only in PostgreSQL (a trigger refuses UPDATE) and hash-chained: each entry stores a SHA-256 of the previous hash and itself, so altering, inserting, reordering or deleting an entry breaks every hash after it. With a signing key, checkpoints sign the newest hash at an interval and at shutdown.
data.policies#Request policies:
A policy refuses inference requests that lack given fields, and replaces the global size limits, for the teams it names and for keys created with it (POST /admin/keys {"policy": "..."}, by a team admin; a key’s own policy wins over its team’s).
require lists body fields (a name or a dotted path); require_tags = true asks for at least one request tag. A refused request gets a 400 naming what is missing, and counts in llmflow_denied_total{reason="policy"}. max_body_bytes and max_response_bytes replace the global limits. The response limit is not applied to streams.
data.request-logs#Per-team request logs:
By default no request log is written for anyone: the spend metadata goes to the accounting store; prompts and completions are forwarded and forgotten, and the gateway’s own log never holds them.
A logging block sends the requests of the teams it names to an export. Each request is one JSON line (time, org, team, project, key id, model, pool, upstream, tokens, cost, latency, status, priority, borrowing, stream, estimated, tags, request id). Content is off: only a block with content = true, an explicit opt-in, adds the request and the answer, each cut at max_content_bytes and marked request_truncated or response_truncated. A team is in at most one block. Lines are batched into gzipped objects under requests//YYYY/MM/DD/.
data.retention#Retention: Entries are kept for ever unless a retention is set per kind (admin, auth for SSO, scim, system). Every prune_interval the gateway deletes the longest prefix of the log that ends at a signed checkpoint and whose every entry is past its kind’s retention: whole segments only, so what remains starts from a signed checkpoint and still verifies. A kind without a retention stops the cut. It never prunes past the newest checkpoint the anchor holds, and never a log that does not verify (audit_prune_refused is raised instead). Each prune is itself an audit.pruned entry.
data.threat-model#What this protects against: Without an anchor With an anchor kept outside an entry edited, inserted, reordered or deleted in the middle detected detected the tail deleted together with the checkpoints that cover it not detected detected an older consistent backup restored (rollback) not detected detected everything deleted not detected detected a log rewritten and re-signed with a stolen key, up to the anchor not detected detected entries after the newest exported checkpoint deleted not detected still open: at most checkpoint_interval plus the export lag a new history signed after the anchor by the holder of the signing key not detected still open Entries and checkpoints live in the same database, which is why an anchor outside it is needed. To narrow what stays open, keep the signing key in OpenBao or Vault, verify with a public key kept elsewhere, and anchor on write-once storage.
data.verifying#Verifying: llmflow-gateway audit keygen -o audit.seed # once; keep the seed in Vault llmflow-gateway audit pubkey -c gateway.hcl # the public key, to keep elsewhere llmflow-gateway audit verify -c gateway.hcl --public-key KEY --anchor export llmflow-gateway audit verify -c gateway.hcl --public-key KEY --anchor file:PATH verify recomputes the chain, checks every checkpoint and, with --anchor, checks the database against the newest checkpoint of the export (or of a file you kept yourself). Take the public key from somewhere the gateway’s operator cannot change. Run without an anchor, verify prints a warning, for the reason below.

data.benchmarking#Benchmarking:
The bench repository holds two small command-line tools, in pure Go, for measuring LLM gateways such as the gateway: gwbench measures the latency a gateway adds, and fakevllm is the upstream it is measured against. Repository →
This page is written from the repository’s README at v0.5.0 (and v0.2.0 for the parts that did not change). v0.5.0 adds a fake slurmrestd and the Slurm end-to-end test (see Slurm discovery). v0.4.0 teaches fakevllm to mimic Anthropic’s API and adds the e2e/anthropic suite (see fakevllm and Anthropic upstream); v0.3.0 added the fakeupstream package (the fake vLLM as a Go package, for tests that embed it with httptest) and the e2e/oidc suite, described on the Identity page. No command or flag of gwbench or fakevllm changed. Since v0.1.0, gwbench has a --direct-model flag (the model name the upstream serves, sent on the direct path), fakevllm is a cobra command line, and an e2e/ suite checks the gateway against a real vLLM (see Verified against a real vLLM).
go install github.com/go-llmflow/bench/cmd/gwbench@latest go install github.com/go-llmflow/bench/cmd/fakevllm@latest
data.control#The control: TestPlantedOverheadIsMeasured puts a proxy that sleeps a known 3 ms and a transparent proxy in front of a test upstream. The instrument must report about 3 ms for the first and about 0 for the second, and separate the two. If it could not see a planted delay, its verdict on real gateways would mean nothing.
data.example#An example: fakevllm --addr 127.0.0.1:18000 --out /tmp/requests.jsonl & llmflow-gateway serve --config llmflow.hcl & # forwards to 127.0.0.1:18000 gwbench llmflow-key --admin http://127.0.0.1:18080 --master-key-file ~/keys/master --out ~/keys/llmflow gwbench run --direct http://127.0.0.1:18000/v1/chat/completions \ --target 'v0.8.0|http://127.0.0.1:18080/v1/chat/completions|'"$HOME"'/keys/llmflow' \ --rounds 2000 --warmup 200 --runs 8 --wait 2h --max-load 4
data.fakevllm#fakevllm:
fakevllm --addr 127.0.0.1:18000 --out requests.jsonl --model fake --reply "ok" Flags: --addr, --out, --model, --reply, --delay, --token-delay, --max-body.
Route Answer GET /v1/models one model, named by --model POST /v1/messages an Anthropic message; with "stream": true, the event sequence message_start, content_block_start, content_block_delta…, content_block_stop, message_delta (with usage.output_tokens), message_stop any other POST an OpenAI chat.completion; with "stream": true, chat.completion.chunk events (role, one chunk per word of --reply, finish), the usage chunk with empty choices when stream_options.include_usage is set, then data: [DONE] Since v0.4.0 the /v1/messages route can mimic Anthropic’s behaviour:
Flag Effect --status N answer every message with that status (429, 529, …) --retry-after S the retry-after header sent with it, in seconds --cache-read N, --cache-write-5m N, --cache-write-1h N prompt-cache tokens reported in usage --workspace ID (or per-key) the workspace named in the response headers --ratelimit-headers send the anthropic-ratelimit-* headers Streams carry a ping event after message_start.
Usage is predictable: one prompt token per whitespace-separated word of the request’s message and system strings, and one completion token per word of --reply. --delay and --token-delay slow the answer and the stream.
Every request is appended to --out (mode 0600) as one JSON line, {"method","path","headers","body"}; a body that is not JSON is recorded as a string. The recording holds the headers as received, Authorization included. That is by design, since it is a witness of what a gateway forwarded. Use test keys only. If the record cannot be written, the request gets a 500, so a test never reads a silent gap as “nothing was forwarded”. Bodies are capped by --max-body (1 MiB; larger ones get a 413).
data.interleaving#Interleaving: Each round sends one request to every target, one at a time, in a fresh random order (seeded with --seed). Drift of the machine (thermal state, a background job, the cache) then spreads evenly over all targets instead of penalising whichever runs last. The first --warmup rounds are discarded.
data.keys#Keys: Keys are read from files, never from the command line or the environment. A KEYFILE may be empty for an open endpoint. gwbench llmflow-key creates an llmflow virtual key through the admin API (--master-key-file) and writes it to a file of mode 0600. Keep key files outside the repository.
data.load#Load gating:
Ratios measured on a busy machine are meaningless. A run starts only when the 1-minute load average is at most --max-load (default 4). With --wait, the tool waits for the load to fall; without it, it refuses at once. A run whose load ends above the limit is discarded, not averaged. --runs kept runs are collected, and their rounds stay paired when they are merged.
The load is read from /proc/loadavg on Linux and from sysctl vm.loadavg on macOS. Elsewhere the tool cannot read it and refuses to measure.
data.pairing#Pairing: A gateway’s overhead in round r is its latency minus the direct latency of the same round. Percentiles are taken over these paired differences, which cancels what both paths share: the client, the loopback and the upstream.

data.results#Dated results:
Overhead is the paired difference against a direct call to the same upstream. Each result is tied to its date and protocol; none is a promise for another machine, another load or another request.
Common to both dates. Machine: Apple M4 Max (Mac16,5), 16 cores, 128 GiB RAM, macOS 27.0.1. Each gateway ran with GOMAXPROCS=1; LiteLLM 1.106.2 ran as one process. Upstream: fakevllm on loopback, answering instantly. Client: gwbench, requests one at a time, target order shuffled every round. Each kept run is 2,000 rounds after a warm-up of 200, and the 1-minute load was at most 4 at its start and at its end.
data.verified-anthropic#Anthropic upstream:
e2e/anthropic (bench v0.4.0) checks the gateway’s Anthropic upstream against fakevllm playing Anthropic. It needs BENCH_GATEWAY_BIN set to a gateway of v0.12.0 or later. It checks that:
the request leaves with the organisation’s key, not the client’s credential, and without the OAuth beta; the PII is masked, and cache_salt and priority are gone, before egress; streams work, and /v1/chat/completions is refused; the spend report, in USD, equals the price list applied to the usage the provider reported; a 429 with retry-after makes the gateway answer 429 itself, for that organisation only. Result: on 2026-10-26 the fake-API suite passes against gateway v0.12.0. It proves the gateway’s behaviour against a fake; it says nothing about Anthropic’s real API. A second test, TestGatewayInFrontOfRealAnthropic, runs only when BENCH_ANTHROPIC_KEY_FILE names a file holding a key (the model is BENCH_ANTHROPIC_MODEL, default claude-haiku-5-5). It was not run for v0.4.0, since no key was available.
data.verified-slurm#Slurm discovery:
Bench v0.5.0 tests the gateway’s Slurm discovery two ways.
A fake slurmrestd, without a cluster. The package fakeupstream provides Slurmrestd: GET /slurm//jobs/ answers the jobs given to SetJobs, in the shape of OPENAPI_JOB_INFO_RESP; job_state is a flag array (["RUNNING"], ["RUNNING","COMPLETING"]); a request must carry X-SLURM-USER-TOKEN set to Token; SetDown(true) simulates an outage (it answers 502).
e2e/slurm_test.go (TestSlurmDiscoveryE2E) runs on a real Slurm node, as root. data.verified-vllm#Verified against a real vL:
The gateway’s design rests on vLLM behaviours read in vLLM’s documentation and source. The e2e/ suite of bench checks them live: it starts llmflow-gateway with freshly generated keys, creates a virtual key per team, and drives it in front of a running vLLM. Without BENCH_VLLM_URL every test skips, so CI runs none of them.
Variable Meaning BENCH_VLLM_URL the chat vLLM (required) BENCH_VLLM_MODEL its model name (default: the first of /v1/models) BENCH_GATEWAY_BIN the llmflow-gateway binary (default: from PATH) BENCH_VLLM_MAX_NUM_SEQS the server’s --max-num-seqs (the scenarios need 2) BENCH_VLLM_KV_SHORTAGE=1 vLLM runs with a tiny KV cache: enables the preemption checks BENCH_VLLM_EMBED_URL, BENCH_VLLM_RERANK_URL optional embedding and score-model servers Setup. vLLM 0.32.1rc1 (nightly CPU image) in arm64 Docker on an Apple M4 Max; models Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (bfloat16), bge-small-en-v1.5 and bge-reranker-base; gateway v0.8.0. The released v0.32.0 arm64 image failed every CPU generation (compute_slot_mapping), which is why the nightly was used; that failure concerns the CPU build only. The gateway configuration is organisation A (two teams, share 0.5) and B (one team, share 0.25) on a pool of capacity 2, so A reserves one slot and every request of B borrows; cache_isolation = "org".
Every ordering check has a control straight to vLLM that must come out the other way, and the cache checks read vLLM’s own counters, never timing.
Check Result Evidence FCFS control, direct pass B3, sent first, served 4.7 s before A1 Header over body pass body 100 and header -100: B3 first; body 100 alone: A1 first Within-share before borrowers pass via the gateway, A1 (sent later) served 5.2 s before B3 KV preemption pass 640-token KV cache, 2 x 384 tokens: the direct control preempts the newest (A1, paused 1 min 35 s); via the gateway the borrower B1 is preempted (1 min 22 s), A1 pauses at most 1.06 s and finishes first Client priority ignored pass body, vllm_xargs, extra_body and header at -100: order unchanged Prefix cache (vLLM’s counters) pass same organisation 768/814; other organisation 0/814; a client’s cache_salt 0; cached content without a salt 0; direct control 768/812 Responses pass GET /v1/responses/{id} through the gateway answers 404; the direct control is readable Messages, tokenize, embeddings, rerank pass complete SSE; 6 tokens on both sides; 384 dimensions; “Paris” ranked first (0.998) Accounting pass vLLM 132 prompt / 44 generated, the gateway charged 132 / 44 vLLM beyond --max-num-seqs pass 6 concurrent requests with 2 slots: six 200, no 429 or 503 Fallback on saturation (gateway v0.11.0, #58) pass two borrowing streams of b1 fill pool cpu (C = 2); the next b1 request is served by chat-spare (X-Llmflow-Model), a1’s within-share request stays on chat; llmflow_fallbacks_total{reason="saturated"} = 1. Run on 2026-10-26 with --max-num-seqs 4 (both pools on one vLLM), with a gateway built from gateway#66, before the v0.11.0 release The vLLM-beyond---max-num-seqs row is why saturation needs its own rule: vLLM queues instead of refusing, so a fallback on an outage never sees a queue. The last row is the check of that rule. TestFallbackOnSaturation needs BENCH_VLLM_MAX_NUM_SEQS=4 (a vLLM started with --max-num-seqs 4) and a gateway of v0.11.0 or later; it skips otherwise.
Not covered: audio transcription (no Whisper model run on CPU) and throughput.
data.what#What is measured:
The question is “how much latency does a gateway add?”, not “how fast is the model”. The upstream must therefore answer as fast as possible: that is fakevllm, which replies instantly. The number reported is a difference between two paths to the same upstream, not a latency.
direct calls the upstream itself. Every other target (--litellm, --llmflow, or --target NAME|URL|KEYFILE, repeatable) is a gateway forwarding to that same upstream.

data.anchors#4. Audit anchors on S3: The admin audit log is hash-chained with signed checkpoints. Its guarantees end at its newest anchor: without an exported anchor, truncation or rollback of the database goes undetected. Anchors can be written to S3 (or Ceph RGW), under Object Lock retention when the bucket has it enabled; create the bucket that way, since MinIO and Ceph require it at creation. Keep the signing key in OpenBao or Vault. See Audit and logging and its threat model.
data.architecture#The architecture: users, coding agents ──► N gateway replicas ──► vLLM instances (virtual keys, JWT, (ha block, mutual TLS ▲ single sign-on) on the internal port) │ each replica follows the │ │ │ running jobs on its own │ └── owner of each pool: a lease ─┐ ▼ ▼ PostgreSQL Slurm (slurmrestd, read only): (accounting, leases, sessions, jobs of account svc_llm, QOS alert outbox, key revocations) service, started and stopped │ by sbatch, scancel, scrontab ▼ S3 with Object Lock (audit anchors) administrators ──► single sign-on through authn-bridge (SAML federations) or an OIDC provider Clients reach the gateway with a virtual key or a JWT; it maps them to an organisation, a team and a project and gives each request a vLLM priority from the institution’s share (Gateway, Identity). vLLM instances run as Slurm jobs of a service account, for example svc_llm with the QOS service. The gateway follows them and never starts or stops one. Several gateway replicas share the pools; PostgreSQL is the only shared component (no etcd, no Redis). Batch and inference share the same GPUs. How Slurm’s Fair Tree, the QOS and preemption split them is the subject of the guide: see Slurm: fair-share, QOS and preemption and Inference.
data.checking#7. Checking a deployment: llmflow-gateway check-config -c validates the configuration and every secret file it names. Run it on each replica’s file. The acceptance tests of the guide: Audit and acceptance. The tools that measure the gateway against a real vLLM, and a real Slurm: Benchmarking. What was audited and attacked: Security.
data.deployment#Deployment:
How the pieces fit on a co-owned GPU cluster, and which page says what. It states the architecture as the gateway’s README gives it and links to the pages that hold the details; it adds no measurement and no recommendation of its own. What the READMEs do not say is marked open, not invented.
Written from the README of gateway v0.16.1 and of bench v0.5.0.
data.identity#5. Identity: authn-bridge and s: Administrators sign in through an OpenID provider. For a SAML federation (RENATER, eduGAIN) the gateway is registered as a client of go-authn/bridge (authn-bridge), an OpenID provider in front of the federation, and sso.issuer points at the bridge. SCIM provisions users and groups. With an ha block the SSO sessions live in PostgreSQL, so they outlive a replica. See Identity.
data.postgresql#1. PostgreSQL:
The one shared component. With the postgres store the gateway needs a spool directory (store.spool_dir, mandatory since v0.10.0): every batch of accounting records is written there and synced before it goes to the database, so records survive an outage within stated bounds (Upgrading to v0.10.0). With an ha block PostgreSQL also holds the pool leases (expiry on PostgreSQL’s own clock), the SSO sessions (sealed, under hashed ids), the soft-budget alert outbox, and carries the key revocations (NOTIFY). The version used by the chaos tests was PostgreSQL 18.
The spool is per process (its cap is per process too); a process that dies leaves its file, and the next process on the directory adopts and stores it. Open: sizing, backup and restore of the database are not in the README.
data.replicas#3. N gateway replicas:
The ha block, off by default. With Slurm discovery (works with ha since v0.15.2) each replica discovers and health-checks on its own, for its own routing, and only the owner’s view sets the pool’s capacity and reservations. This assembled configuration (replicas differ by replica_id, listen and advertise) passes llmflow-gateway check-config v0.16.1 with the key, DSN, secret and token files present:
store { kind = "postgres" dsn_file = "/run/secrets/dsn" spool_dir = "/var/spool/llmflow" } ha { listen = "10.0.0.5:9444" advertise = "10.0.0.5:9444" peer_networks = ["10.0.0.0/24"] secret_file = "/run/secrets/ha" } org "instA" { share = 1 team "a-physics" {} } pool "gpu" { capacity = 0 } model "llama" { upstream_model = "meta/llama-3.3-70b" pool = "gpu" key_file = "/etc/llmflow/vllm.key" slurm { url = "https://slurmrestd.cluster:6820" token_file = "/etc/llmflow/slurm.jwt" accounts = ["svc_llm"] partitions = ["gpu"] } } (The same file with the paths of the test machine; master and cache-salt keys omitted above.)
Mutual TLS between the replicas is optional: tls_cert_file, tls_key_file and tls_ca_file (all three or none), PEM files or vault: references, with tls_server_name naming the DNS name in each replica’s certificate. Use v0.16.1 or later: v0.16.0 rejected every multi-line PEM file. With v0.16.1, check-config accepts real PEM files (an EC P-256 CA and a certificate for llmflow-ha, tested on 2026-10-26) and refuses a certificate whose key does not match. The key file must not be readable by group or others. Not verified here: a live handshake between two replicas. See High availability.
Behaviour in a failover, the chaos results and the open items: High availability. A killed owner was replaced in 1.3 s with no request failed; a partitioned owner never overlapped the new one (805 samples). Without a reachable owner a request is admitted at the lowest borrowing priority, or refused with 503 under on_owner_unreachable = "reject". Per-key rate limits are still counted per replica. Put the replicas behind a load balancer of your choice; the README does not prescribe one. Open: the latency a forwarded admission adds, with and without mutual TLS, is not measured.
data.reports#6. Reports and reconciliation: What finance sees, and how it is set beside Slurm’s own accounting (sreport): Finance reports. The PDF is written by go-pdfkit.
data.slurm-jobs#2. vLLM as Slurm jobs:
A slurm block inside a model: the job-name convention llmflow::[:], the allowed accounts, partitions and users, admission after /health and /v1/models, drain on job end or after three failed health checks, the pool’s capacity recomputed and audited, fail-closed after stale_after.
One instance, as a job (the key goes in VLLM_API_KEY, never --api-key):
#!/bin/bash #SBATCH --job-name=llmflow:llama:8000:8 #SBATCH --account=svc_llm --qos=service --partition=gpu #SBATCH --nodes=1 --gres=gpu:4 --exclusive --time=7-00:00:00 #SBATCH --signal=B:TERM@120 VLLM_API_KEY=$(cat /etc/llmflow/vllm.key); export VLLM_API_KEY exec vllm serve meta/llama-3.3-70b --served-model-name meta/llama-3.3-70b \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --tensor-parallel-size 4 Day and night, with scrontab (needs ScronParameters=enable): the jobs end at 20:00, the gateway drains them, the pool shrinks and the reservations follow, so the GPUs can be lent to a borrowing QOS; at 07:00 the new jobs are admitted as soon as vLLM answers.
#SCRON --account=svc_llm --qos=service --partition=service -t 0:05:00 0 7 * * 1-5 sbatch /opt/llmflow/vllm-llama.sbatch #SCRON --account=svc_llm --qos=service --partition=service -t 0:05:00 0 20 * * 1-5 scancel --account=svc_llm --name=llmflow:llama:8000:8 The node’s vLLM port must be reachable by the gateway replicas only (firewall): /metrics is unauthenticated, and the key protects /v1 only. slurmrestd needs AuthAltTypes=auth/jwt; the gateway’s token is issued with scontrol token username=svc_llm lifespan=..., read at start only, so its lifespan must outlast your restart cycle. Full text, safety rules and the metrics: Slurm discovery. What was tested on a real Slurm: Benchmarking. Open: the README’s tests used a small CPU model on one node; no GPU node and no multi-node tensor-parallel job were tested.

data.dimensions#Who is charged: organisation,:
The report groups by any of org, lab, team, project, user, key, model, pool, tag and day. Two levels are new in v0.13.0 and one is now filled by clients:
lab is optional, set on a team (team "physics-1" { lab = "physics" }). It is an accounting level only; access control does not use it. It is stamped on each record when the request is made, so moving a team to another lab later does not rewrite the past. user is the key’s owner, or a JWT’s username, or a stable synthetic id. Never a token. project is named by the client in a header, X-Llmflow-Project, because coding agents do not say which project a request belongs to. See Project attribution and, for the client side, Coding agents. A project the key may not use gets a generic 403. The drill-down follows the same order: organisation, lab, team, project, user.
attribution { project_header = "X-Llmflow-Project" default_project = "general" } org "etabA" { share = 0.5 team "physics-1" { lab = "physics" } team "chem-1" { lab = "chemistry" } } This block passes llmflow-gateway check-config v0.16.1 (with the key files present, and a pool and a model around it). Existing configurations stay valid: a lab is an attribute of a team, not a new nesting.
data.exports#Exports:
From the links on the page, or from the API:
GET /admin/export?from=2026-10-01&to=2026-11-01&format=csv|xlsx|pdf[&group_by=org,lab,team,project,user] Format What the file holds csv the spend report (default grouping org,lab,team,project,user,model,pool), with cost and unit columns xlsx a Summary sheet (the period, totals per unit against the previous period), a Reconciliation sheet (inference against Slurm batch GPU-hours per organisation), then one sheet per grouping: org, lab, team, project, user, model, pool, tag, day. Numbers are typed, each cost column names its unit (Cost (GPU-hours), Cost (USD)) pdf a management summary: the period, totals per unit, totals per level (org, lab, team, project; the ten largest) with pie charts, the daily trend, and the reconciliation table An export shows what the report shows the same person. Each download is written to the audit log with kind export (who, their roles, the query, the format, the size, the status), refusals included. Bounds: at most 366 days, at most 100,000 rows at the finest grouping (HTTP 413 beyond), and the 60-second deadline.
What an export cannot carry:
CSV. A cell that begins with =, +, -, @, a tab or a carriage return is prefixed with ', so a spreadsheet does not read a label as a formula. XLSX. The writer has no formula at all; such strings are marked as text. PDF. Every label is drawn as glyphs, in one embedded font. The file carries no action, link, script or attachment. Labels lose their control and bidi-format characters and are clipped; the file name is built from the dates only. The writers are fuzzed (FuzzExportWriters). From the command line, llmflow-gateway export writes the same report as CSV or parsable2 (see the gateway page). Since v0.13.1 it has the API’s bounds: at most 366 days, 100,000 rows and 60 s in the store. An operator raises them explicitly with --max-days, --max-rows and --timeout. Every run is written to the audit log (kind export, actor cli:) before the store is read; a run with a raised bound does not start when that entry cannot be written, and a run within the defaults prints a warning instead. (Take v0.14.1 or later, not v0.13.1: see which tag to take.)

The binary grew, then shrank. In v0.13.0 to v0.15.1 go-pdfkit’s root package pulled in a widget toolkit the export never used. data.page#The page: /ui/reports:
The page is part of the admin web UI: it needs an sso block and a signed-in administrator, it holds no privilege of its own, and an organisation administrator sees their organisation only. It shows:
A period, with date pickers and shortcuts (last 7 days, last 30 days, this month, last month, this year). Dates are UTC and the end is excluded. At most 366 days. A grouping over any dimension above, including day. A drill-down. In an org grouping each row links to its labs, then teams, projects, users and models. The filters in force are listed and each can be removed. The previous period of the same length, side by side: the amount and the change. data.slurm#Reconciling with Slurm:
The gateway knows the GPU-hours of the inference it served. Slurm knows the GPU-hours of the batch jobs on the same cluster. Next to each other, per organisation, they say how the shared GPUs were really used: on the Reports page and in the XLSX and PDF exports. This is optional.
The input is the output of sreport:
sreport -P cluster AccountUtilizationByUser -T gres/gpu -t Hours start=2026-10-01 end=2026-11-01 Either a file the gateway reads whenever it builds a report, or a file uploaded with an export (POST /admin/export?...&format=xlsx|pdf, the report as a text/plain body, or the form on the Reports page):
slurm { sreport_file = "/var/lib/llmflow/sreport.txt" # optional; absolute path accounts = { "phys-a" = "etabA" } # optional; Slurm account -> organisation } This block passes llmflow-gateway check-config v0.16.1 (with the file present).
How the file is read:
Delimited layouts (-P, -p, or a comma-separated file with the same header) and sreport’s default fixed-width table. Prefer -P: the fixed width truncates long names with +. Only account totals count (rows without a login), for the organisation accounts names or, failing that, the organisation of the same name. The unit comes from the “Usage reported in …” line (minutes by default, hours or seconds). A report in percent is refused; rows of another TRES are skipped. The period sreport printed is shown next to the table, so a mismatch with the report’s period is visible. Look at it before trusting a comparison. The file is untrusted: at most 1 MiB, 50,000 lines of 4 KiB, 32 columns, finite non-negative numbers, UTF-8. Every refusal is an error: 400 for an upload; for a configured file that cannot be read, a generic 500 and a log line (the path is never shown). The parser is fuzzed (FuzzSreport). An organisation’s batch usage is shown to whoever may view that organisation (organisation viewers and administrators, proxy roles). Team-level roles see none.

data.aborted#Aborted requests: vLLM’s usage chunk comes last. When the client leaves before it, the gateway stops reading (vLLM is not kept generating for nobody) and charges an estimate: prompt bytes / 4 plus the content deltas already forwarded. The record is flagged, in an estimated_requests column of the spend reports and in PostgreSQL. The estimate undercounts tool-call and reasoning tokens.

Admin routes take Authorization: Bearer or a user’s llma-... token.

data.admin-ui#Admin web UI:
With an sso block, /ui/ serves a web console for administrators (/admin/login?next=ui signs in and lands there). It is server-rendered HTML with no JavaScript, under a strict policy on every /ui/ response:
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; style-src 'self'; img-src 'self'; form-action 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'; base-uri 'none' plus X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, Referrer-Policy: no-referrer and Cache-Control: no-store. The one stylesheet is served by the gateway; no third-party asset is loaded.
Page What it does Keys list per team; create (the secret is shown once, on a page that is not cached), rotate with a grace period, revoke Budgets budgets with spent and limit; set and delete Spend GPU-hours, requests and tokens over a period, grouped by organisation, team, project, key, model, pool or tag Reports (since v0.13.0) the finance view of the spend report: period, drill-down, previous period, charts, exports, Slurm reconciliation. See Finance reports Fair share live state per pool: reservation, in flight, borrowing, level fairshare and rank Audit entries page by page, and a button that verifies the chain (status of the checkpoints and of the anchor) The UI holds no privilege of its own: every page calls the admin API’s handlers in-process with the signed-in person, so it has the same RBAC as the API (an organisation administrator sees their organisation only) and every change is audited as through the API. Only an SSO session is accepted; without an sso block /ui/ answers 404. Two admin routes were added for it: GET /admin/audit?from=&limit= and POST /admin/audit/verify (proxy admins and viewers only). The verification uses the gateway’s own key; for an independent check use llmflow-gateway audit verify with a public key kept elsewhere (see Audit and logging).
data.anthropic#Anthropic as an upstream (opt-:
Several institutions can share one Anthropic organisation’s API usage through the gateway, with its keys, budgets, fair share, audit and guardrails. The only path is an Anthropic API key under the Commercial Terms: pooling Claude Pro or Max subscriptions is forbidden by the Consumer Terms, and Claude Code’s documentation forbids routing requests through Free, Pro or Max credentials on behalf of users (legal and compliance). The gateway therefore never relays a subscription: it drops the OAuth anthropic-beta capability and never forwards a client’s Authorization or x-api-key. This is not legal advice: check your institution’s contracts with your DPO.
This block, from the gateway’s examples/anthropic.hcl with this page’s names, passes llmflow-gateway check-config v0.16.1 (with the key files present, and the organisations, the b300 pool and the local llama-3.3-70b model of that example around it):
pool "anthropic" { capacity = 32 } # concurrent requests the institutions share at Anthropic model "claude-sonnet" { provider = "anthropic" upstream_model = "claude-sonnet-5-5" pool = "anthropic" allow_external = true orgs = ["instA", "instB"] anthropic_betas = ["context-management-2025-06-27"] cost { unit = "USD" price_date = "2026-10-26" input_per_mtok = 2 output_per_mtok = 10 cached_per_mtok = 0.1 cache_write_5m_per_mtok = 2.5 cache_write_1h_per_mtok = 4 } upstream "api" { base_url = "https://api.anthropic.com" } org_key "instA" { key_file = "/etc/llmflow/anthropic-instA.key" } org_key "instB" { key_file = "/etc/llmflow/anthropic-instB.key" } fallbacks = ["llama-3.3-70b"] fallback_on = ["unavailable"] } guardrail "pii" { type = "pii" orgs = ["instA", "instB"] } guardrail "secrets" { type = "hide_secrets" orgs = ["instA", "instB"] } (The model names, prices and price_date are the README’s example; read the current price list and put its date in price_date.) What check-config enforces:
allow_external = true is required, because prompts leave the site, with an explicit orgs or teams allow-list (others get 404) and https. external_requires_guardrails (top level, default true): every allowed organisation or team needs pre-call pii and hide_secrets guardrails, masking or blocking and fail-closed. They are checked at configuration time and again on every request, which answers 503 when they are missing. One API key per organisation (org_key) when more than one may use the model. Anthropic’s prompt cache is isolated per workspace (the README quotes the prompt caching page, read on 2026-10-26), which is the timing side channel that cache_salt closes for vLLM; Anthropic accepts no salt. Two organisations naming the same key file are refused, and if two ever resolve to the same workspace (anthropic-workspace-id on the answers) both are refused with 503. With cache_isolation = "none", one key may serve everybody, and the residual risk is a shared cache between institutions. An external model is never a fallback target and never shares a pool with vLLM models. Routes. /v1/messages only, JSON and streaming. /v1/chat/completions and the other routes answer 400 for an Anthropic model, because Anthropic’s OpenAI-compatibility layer “is not considered a long-term or production-ready solution”. A client may authenticate with Authorization: Bearer llmf-... or x-api-key: llmf-..., as Anthropic SDKs and Claude Code do.
/v1/messages/count_tokens (since v0.12.1) is sent to Anthropic’s endpoint with the organisation’s key and the same filtered headers. It is not charged: Anthropic says token counting “is free to use”. It is rate limited per key like every route. The pre-call pii and hide_secrets guardrails still mask the prompt, because a count also sends it off the site, and the count is then that of the prompt /v1/messages really sends. Anthropic rate-limits counting separately from message creation, so a 429 on a count is passed through without starting the organisation’s messages back-off, and a messages back-off does not stop the counts. A shared workspace refuses both, and an organisation that is not allowed gets 404.
What reaches Anthropic. Headers are rebuilt: x-api-key is the organisation’s key; anthropic-version is the client’s if allow-listed; anthropic-beta carries the allow-listed values only (add the betas your users need, or "*"; never an OAuth one); no priority, request id or trace context is sent. The body goes through the same rewrite as for vLLM. Back to the client go the provider’s request-id and retry-after, but not its anthropic-ratelimit-* headers, which describe the shared organisation’s usage.
Back-off. The pool’s capacity is the concurrency the institutions share at Anthropic, apportioned by their shares. A 429 or 529 starts a back-off for that organisation, for retry-after seconds (at most 10 minutes; 5 seconds when the header is absent). During it, requests are not sent: they go to the model’s fallbacks (a local vLLM group) when fallback_on includes "unavailable", or get 429 with Retry-After. Other organisations are not affected.
Accounting uses Anthropic’s usage fields (input, cache reads, cache writes split by 5-minute and 1-hour lifetime, output), each priced at its own rate from the cost block, in USD, with its price date.
data.architecture#Architecture: clients (OpenAI SDKs, Authorization: Bearer llmf-...) | v llmflow-gateway 1 auth: virtual key -> team (SHA-256, constant-time, cached) 2 body <= max_body_bytes, JSON re-encoded, client priority fields stripped, per-tenant cache_salt set 3 budget (GPU-hours per day / week / month), fail-closed by default 4 per-key RPM / TPM / max in-flight 5 fair share: within reservation -> priority 0/1, borrowing -> 10 and more 6 route: least in-flight healthy upstream, retry before the first byte 7 stream SSE event by event, capture usage 8 cost -> budget counter, fair-share usage, async PostgreSQL record | v headers built from scratch: Authorization (internal key), X-Vllm-Priority vLLM x N (--scheduling-policy priority --api-key ..., reachable only from the gateway) Packages: fairshare (the algorithm, no I/O), openai (request rewrite, SSE usage capture), store (memory and PostgreSQL), gateway (HTTP server), config, and cmd/llmflow-gateway (cobra command line).
data.attribution#Project attribution, labs an:
Coding clients do not say which project a request belongs to. Claude Code sends no project header of its own, but it sends whatever ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS holds; Continue sends the headers of requestOptions.headers. A request can therefore name its project in a header (X-Llmflow-Project by default), and a team can carry an optional lab:
attribution { project_header = "X-Llmflow-Project" # the default default_project = "general" # optional } org "etabA" { share = 0.5 team "physics-1" { lab = "physics" } # optional lab: org, lab, team, project } This block passes llmflow-gateway check-config v0.16.1 (with the key files present, and a pool and a model around it).
What the header may name. A project name, looked up in the key’s own team only: another team’s or organisation’s project cannot even be named. The project must exist and be enabled; a key pinned to a project accepts only that one. For a key with an owner, the owner must still hold a stored member, team_admin, org_admin or proxy_admin role on the team; for a JWT the team comes from its verified map. Every refusal is the same generic 403 (“project not allowed for this key”), counted in llmflow_denied_total{reason="project"}. Without the header, the key’s project applies, then default_project if the team has a project of that name, else none. The effective project is charged, budgeted, written to the request log and recorded. The lookups read state loaded with the budgets, so the request path does not read the store. SSO roles do not count. A role that comes only from SSO ID-token claims is not stored, so it does not satisfy the check: grant the role in the gateway, or through SCIM. Two reporting dimensions. lab is an accounting level only (RBAC does not use it), stamped on each record at request time, so moving a team to another lab does not rewrite history. user is the key’s owner, or a JWT’s username when it is a valid gateway user name, otherwise the JWT’s stable synthetic key id; never a token. A lab is an attribute rather than a nesting so that every existing configuration stays valid. How a coding agent sets the header: Coding agents.
data.audit-2026-10-26#Security audit of 2026-:
A security audit and a chaos run of v0.8.0 were made on 2026-10-26. The fixes below are released in v0.9.0; each has a test that fails without the fix. The full account (method, findings A1 to A9, chaos results, residual risks) is on the Security page.
A1, multimodal uuids on every route (medium). They were scoped per tenant on chat completions and Responses only. On /v1/rerank, /v2/rerank, /tokenize and /v1/embeddings the client’s uuid reached vLLM unchanged, so a tenant could refer to another tenant’s cached media (and probe it through a rerank score or a token count). The walk now follows every shape vLLM accepts, and a fuzz target, FuzzScopeEveryRoute, checks every route. A2, a client that never reads its answer (medium). It held its in-flight slot, its fair-share grant and up to max_response_bytes of memory for ever. Every response now has a write deadline of max_request_duration plus 5 s. A3, re-enabling a disabled user (high). An organisation admin could re-enable a disabled proxy_admin by creating the user again. Only a proxy admin may now. A test, TestAuthzMatrix, covers every admin route against 12 principals; no other cross-organisation hole was found on the 39 routes. A4, disabled teams (low). A disabled team or project now disables its keys, including one created during the disable, and the cached JWTs of its people, at once. A5, export queues (medium). With the export target down and content logging on, up to 8 GiB of logs could pile up in memory. A queue is now also bounded to 256 MiB, and what is dropped is counted and alerted. A6 and A7, store faults (medium and low). Key lookups and tool-list reads give up after 5 s (503), a budget refresh after 30 s, and admin, UI and SCIM requests after 60 s, instead of hanging when PostgreSQL is partitioned. Two replicas can now start together on an empty database. Chaos tests cover PostgreSQL down, partitioned and restarted, an upstream restart, a key rotation under load, two replicas, and a clock stepping back. The loss of usage records during an accounting outage was an open defect (limitation 6), fixed in v0.10.0 by the durable accounting spool.

Static evaluation. The file is decoded with no evaluation context: no variables, no functions. env.HOME, file("/etc/shadow") or "${x}" are errors, so a configuration cannot read the environment or other files. Quoted strings are templates. A literal ${ must be written $${, and a literal %{ must be written %%{. This applies to every value, URLs, paths and model names included. Labelled blocks for named things: org, team, pool, model, upstream. Duplicate labels are errors. Teams nest inside their organisation. Every diagnostic carries file:line:column; check-config prints them one per line. Secrets only by file (master_key_file, metrics_token_file, store.dsn_file, key_file, cache_salt_key_file, and so on). An upstream URL with credentials is rejected. Durations are strings in Go syntax ("30s", "168h"). Absent and zero differ: retries = 0 disables retries, leaving it out takes the default. The parser is fuzzed (FuzzParse): the configuration is treated as untrusted input. Cost of a request, in GPU-hours: ((prompt - cached) x input + cached x cached_price + completion x output) / 10^6, from the usage vLLM reports.
data.cost-units#Cost units (since v0.12.0):
A cost has a unit. vLLM models cost GPU-hours by default; a model can be priced in a currency, with the date its prices were read (unit = "USD", price_date). GPU-hours and a currency are never added together: a budget carries a unit ({"kind":"org","name":"instA","unit":"USD","period":"month","max_cost":500}) and counts only the requests of models priced in that unit; a spend report is split by unit, with cost and unit columns (CSV and parsable2 gain them at the end); currency costs go to the metric llmflow_cost_total{team,pool,unit}, while llmflow_gpu_hours_total stays GPU-hours only. A pool must not mix units (check-config refuses it).
Upgrading to v0.12.0. PostgreSQL gains a unit column on llmflow_usage and on llmflow_budgets_v2, whose primary key becomes (kind, name, model, unit). Existing rows are GPU-hours. The migration runs at start-up, once: back the database up first, as for any schema change.
data.fair-share-with-borrowing#How fair-share:
A pool has a capacity C: the concurrency it sustains without preemption, measured externally. Each organisation owns an integer reservation, shared by all its teams and projects, obtained by apportioning C over the shares with the largest-remainder (Hamilton) method, so reservations never sum to more than C (C = 256 gives A 208 and B 48).
For every request:
Situation Priority sent to vLLM the organisation has fewer within-share requests in flight than its reservation 0 interactive, 1 batch otherwise (borrowing) 10 + 10 x rank + class, rank at most 9 Among borrowers, rank is the dense rank of the organisation’s level fairshare LF = S / U (Slurm Fair Tree): the most under-served has rank 0, so the most over-served borrower gets the largest number, is admitted last and is preempted first. Usage is the cost actually consumed, charged when a request finishes and decayed with a half-life (the exact exponential, of which Slurm’s 1 - 0.693/hl is the first-order expansion).
vLLM’s v1 scheduler keeps waiting requests in a min-heap on (priority, arrival_time); when a running request runs out of KV blocks, the running request with the largest (priority, arrival_time) is preempted; a waiting request never preempts a running one. A within-share request is therefore admitted before any borrower and is never the victim while a borrower runs. The guide explains vLLM’s priority semantics from its source.
Two choices were forced by the simulator: the reservation test counts within-share requests in flight (not all requests), and usage is charged at release (not from time in flight, since a request waiting in vLLM’s queue consumes nothing).

data.fallbacks#Fallbacks:
A model group can name fallbacks, tried in order (at most 4, not a guard model, not itself):
model "llama-70b" { pool = "b300" fallbacks = ["llama-8b"] fallback_on = ["unavailable", "saturated"] # default ["unavailable"] saturation_waiting = 4 # optional # ... } "unavailable" (the default): an outage. Before anything has reached the client, a request moves to the next fallback when no upstream of the group took it, or when vLLM answered 429 or 503.
"saturated" (since v0.11.0, issue #58). Measured on 2026-10-26, a vLLM above its --max-num-seqs does not refuse: it queues the requests and answers 200 (six requests over the limit, six 200s, no 429 or 503). So the gateway decides saturation itself:
A pool is saturated when it already had capacity (C) requests in flight when the request arrived. With saturation_waiting = N, it is also saturated when the group’s upstreams report N or more requests waiting in vllm:num_requests_waiting (read from each upstream’s /metrics, which vLLM serves without authentication, so keep its ports internal; an upstream that cannot be read counts as unknown, never as saturated). Only a borrowing request moves. A request within its organisation’s share keeps its reservation and queues in its own pool; the README states this as a property, tested over 200 random schedules and failing on a planted regression. Only into room, and the check of the target pool’s room and the admission there are one atomic step. A request moves at most once; with no room anywhere it waits in its own pool, so two saturated groups naming each other cannot ping-pong. In both cases the target must be in the team’s model list and within its budgets. The request acquires in the target’s pool (so it gets its organisation’s priority there), is rewritten for the target, and is charged and recorded under the model that served it. The response carries X-Llmflow-Model, and llmflow_fallbacks_total{from,to,reason} counts the moves, reason being unavailable or saturated. Any other answer, a 400 for instance, is final.
Upgrading to v0.11.0. llmflow_fallbacks_total has a new reason label (breaking for a dashboard or an alert that matches its labels exactly). And fallback_on now also governs the outage case: a model set to ["saturated"] alone no longer falls back when its upstream is unavailable. The real-vLLM check is on the Benchmarking page.
