It replaces LiteLLM for that role and adds fair-share scheduling with reservation and borrowing, mapped onto vLLM’s own priority scheduler. Repository →
data.ha#High availability: several replicas (:
Without an ha block nothing changes: one replica, the fair-share state in its memory. With one, several replicas share the pools and PostgreSQL stays the only shared component (no etcd, no Redis). Design discussion: issue #74.
store { kind = "postgres" # required by ha dsn_file = "/run/secrets/dsn" spool_dir = "/var/spool/llmflow" } ha { replica_id = "gw-1" # optional, default the host name listen = "10.0.0.5:9444" # internal port, replicas only advertise = "10.0.0.5:9444" # default: listen (an IP literal) peer_networks = ["10.0.0.0/24"] # owners are dialled only there secret_file = "/run/secrets/ha" # shared, at least 32 bytes lease_ttl = "6s" # renewed every third heartbeat = "1s" # grant reports to owners forward_timeout = "250ms" usage_persist = "10s" on_owner_unreachable = "lowest_priority" # or "reject" (503) } This block passes llmflow-gateway check-config v0.16.1 (with the key, DSN and secret files present, and organisations, a pool and a model around it). check-config also checks the block: the postgres store, an advertised IP literal inside peer_networks, heartbeat at most a third of lease_ttl, forward_timeout at most a heartbeat, and a secret of at least 32 bytes.
The optional mutual-TLS lines go in the same ha block (since v0.16.0; use v0.16.1 or later, see below):
ha { # ... as above, then: tls_cert_file = "/etc/llmflow/ha-cert.pem" # this replica's certificate (PEM) tls_key_file = "/etc/llmflow/ha-key.pem" # its key: one PEM block, mode 0600 tls_ca_file = "/etc/llmflow/ha-ca.pem" # signs every replica tls_server_name = "llmflow-ha" # the default; in the certificate's SAN } This form is validated by check-config v0.16.1 with real PEM files: an EC P-256 CA and a replica certificate with the DNS name llmflow-ha, generated for the test, as multi-line PEMs (the key file at mode 0600, which the loader requires). The repository’s README also shows the certificate and key as vault: references, such as vault:secret/llmflow/ha#cert; the loader accepts both a file path and a vault: reference, and that form needs a vault block which is not shown here and was not run. The certificate file may carry intermediates after the leaf, the CA file may bundle several CAs, and check-config refuses a certificate outside its validity period.
Use v0.16.1 or later for mutual TLS. v0.16.0 read these three values with the one-line secret reader and rejected every multi-line PEM file: check-config v0.16.1 answered ha tls_cert_file: secret ... holds more than one line for a real certificate. Fixed in v0.16.1 (the PEM-aware loader). What this page has verified is check-config acceptance of real files; I have not seen a live handshake between two replicas, and the repository’s own tests of refused peers (no certificate, another CA, plain HTTP, another server name) are the repository’s, not re-run here.
One owner per pool. Each pool’s fair share (in-flight counts, reservations, decayed usage) is decided by one replica at a time: the holder of the pool’s lease row in PostgreSQL. The lease’s epoch is a fencing token that grows at every change of owner. Expiry is computed with PostgreSQL’s clock, never a replica’s, and a takeover is one conditional statement, so of several replicas racing on an expired lease exactly one wins. No split brain. The owner decides only until the monotonic time at which its last successful renewal started, plus 0.9 x lease_ttl; PostgreSQL cannot hand the lease to anyone before that renewal expires. An owner cut from PostgreSQL therefore stops deciding before another replica can start. Its usage writes are fenced at the storage, and a replica that has seen a newer epoch refuses an older owner’s answer. Forwarding the decision, not the request. The other replicas send acquire and release to the owner over the internal port, and still send the request to vLLM themselves: one small round trip per admission (the release is asynchronous), and the streamed answer does not cross a second gateway. Every message is signed with HMAC-SHA256 (key derived from secret_file), bound to the sender’s instance, a sequence number and a timestamp (5 minutes of clock difference accepted); replays are refused with a sliding window per instance (RFC 4303, 3.4.3). The owner’s address is read from the database and dialled only inside peer_networks, without redirects, with forward_timeout. Mutual TLS on the internal port (since v0.16.0, working files since v0.16.1), optional. With tls_cert_file, tls_key_file and tls_ca_file (file paths or vault: references, all three or none: check-config refuses a partial set) the channel runs over mutual TLS 1.3. Each replica presents its certificate, accepts only peers the CA signed, and checks that the server’s certificate carries tls_server_name (default llmflow-ha; replicas are dialled by IP). The HMAC signatures stay: they bind each answer to its request and refuse replays. Tested in the repository: a peer without a certificate, with one from another CA, speaking plain HTTP, or expecting another server name gets nothing, even though it holds the HMAC secret. The cost (a handshake per kept-alive connection, then AES-GCM on bodies of a few hundred bytes) is not measured yet. Failover. Every replica reports its live grants to the owner each heartbeat. A new owner (epoch + 1) restores the decayed usage the previous one persisted every usage_persist, adopts the grants the surviving replicas report, and counts the previous owner’s last persisted in-flight requests as phantoms: a safety margin that expires after limits.max_request_duration and shrinks as reports account for them. Without a reachable owner (the seconds of a failover) a request is admitted at the lowest borrowing priority, which cannot take anyone’s reservation, or refused with 503 under on_owner_unreachable = "reject". Such a request cannot move to a fallback on saturation, because the pool’s room is unknown. Also shared through PostgreSQL. SSO logins and sessions (the row key is the SHA-256 of the cookie, the content sealed with AES-256-GCM under a key derived from secret_file); soft-budget alerts, through an outbox table, delivered at least once with the same Idempotency-Key; key revocations, broadcast with NOTIFY and LISTEN so every replica drops its cached identities at once. Metrics. llmflow_ha_owner, llmflow_ha_epoch, llmflow_ha_local_grants (per pool), llmflow_ha_unowned_total, llmflow_inflight_phantoms (per pool and organisation) and llmflow_ha_revocations_total. The fair-share gauges are published by the owner only. Chaos tests (real PostgreSQL 18, 2026-10-26, from the repository’s README):
Fault Result Owner killed with SIGKILL mid-traffic (lease_ttl 1.5 s) survivor owner after 1.3 s, epoch 1 to 2; 207 requests served meanwhile, 0 failed (203 of them at the lowest priority before the takeover) Owner partitioned from PostgreSQL (lease_ttl 900 ms) the old owner stops deciding 804 ms after the cut, the other replica owns from 904 ms; 0 of 805 samples with two owners; it does not take the lease back after the heal Two replicas racing for a lease (8 claimants x 20 rounds) exactly one owner each time Clock skew of +/- 2 minutes on one replica ownership does not move, forwarding works A key revoked on one replica while cached on the other (key_cache_ttl 1 h) refused on the other replica after 3 ms SSO login started on replica A, callback on B, B killed, session used on C the session is served by C; the state cannot be replayed The same soft-budget alert queued by two replicas one delivery Random partitions, kills and restarts of 4 replicas under traffic, 8 s never two owners at one epoch, over 14,000 to 27,000 decisions per run Not measured, and open. The added latency of a forwarded admission is not measured yet (the machine’s load was above the gate’s limit); a Go benchmark compares a single replica, the owner and a forwarded admission. Per-key rate limits (rpm, tpm, max_inflight) are still counted per replica: N replicas allow up to N times the limit. The fencing token is checked by PostgreSQL and by the replicas, not by vLLM, so a decision an owner made just before a long pause can still reach vLLM. Without the tls_* files the internal channel is authenticated but not encrypted: keep it on a private network, or set them (see above). Since v0.15.2 an ha block can be combined with Slurm discovery.
data.hierarchy#Hierarchy and roles:
The tree mirrors a Slurm account tree: organisation (institution) → team (lab) → project → key. Budgets can be set on every scope (organisation, team, project, key, tag), and for one model group. Administration is delegated by role:
Role Scope May proxy_admin everything everything the master key may proxy_viewer everything read every listing, report and fair-share state org_admin one organisation manage its teams, projects, keys, budgets and users below it team_admin one team manage its projects and keys, grant member and viewer on the team member one team create keys (owned by the member), list and revoke their own keys viewer one organisation or team read its teams, projects, keys (no secrets), budgets and spend Users authenticate with admin tokens (llma-..., 256 random bits, stored as SHA-256, shown once). Nobody can grant a role above their own scope. Teams can restrict which model groups they may use.
data.limitations#Limitations:
Open defects of v0.16.1, as the repository lists them:
Rate limits and the key cache are per process. Since v0.14.0 the fair-share state is shared between replicas with an ha block (see High availability); without one, run one gateway replica per pool, since several would each grant the full reservation. Per-key rpm, tpm and max_inflight limits are still counted per replica (N replicas allow up to N times the limit). Without an ha block, a revocation reaches another replica’s key cache after key_cache_ttl (with one, at once by NOTIFY). During a failover (up to lease_ttl) requests are admitted at the lowest priority without an owner’s decision; a new owner’s safety margin is the in-flight count persisted up to usage_persist earlier; the fencing token is checked by PostgreSQL and by the replicas, not by vLLM. Without the tls_* files (mutual TLS, usable from v0.16.1) the internal channel is authenticated, not encrypted. Budgets lag. The cost is known when a request ends, so a burst of long requests can overspend by what is in flight. Several gateways see each other’s spend only at their next refresh. Priority is fixed at admission. A borrowing request already queued in vLLM keeps its priority when its organisation drops back under its reservation, and teams inside an organisation share its reservation without sub-shares of their own. vLLM has no API to re-prioritise a queued request. Aborted requests are charged with an estimate (see above). Prefix-cache isolation is per scope, not absolute (see above). Accounting drops records only when its bounds are reached. A record is dropped when the in-memory queue (queue_size) is full, and lost when the durable spool (spool_max_bytes) is full or cannot be written and the store refuses it too (counted in llmflow_accounting_failed_total, alerted as accounting_records_lost). A record still in the queue when the process dies (at most about 1 s of traffic) is lost. Everything that reached the spool survives a store outage and a crash. Budgets count the cost until the next refresh only. No TLS in the gateway: put it behind a TLS proxy. The admin API shares the client listener. /v1/responses is served statelessly only (see above). C is static configuration; the gateway does not measure or adapt it. Admin principals are read from the store on every admin request, with no cache: role changes apply at once, but the admin API fails with the store. Soft-budget alert retries live in memory. Each channel (webhook, SMTP) is retried on its own, up to 6 attempts with exponential backoff; a 4xx other than 408 and 429 is not retried; every webhook attempt carries the same Idempotency-Key. A gateway stopped mid-retry does not resume: the period is already marked as alerted. (With an ha block alerts go through an outbox table in PostgreSQL and survive a restart.) Without an ha block, SSO sessions live in one replica’s memory: behind several replicas, use sticky sessions. With one, they are in PostgreSQL. A person holding a JWT cannot be revoked individually: disable the team, change the map blocks, or revoke at the identity provider; a token already verified stays cached until its exp or key_cache_ttl. SCIM does not expand nested groups, and a provisioned role on a team that does not exist is logged, not created. The audit log’s guarantees end at its newest anchor. Without an anchor export, truncation, rollback and deletion of the database go undetected; with one, what happened after the newest exported checkpoint can still be removed, and a stolen signing key can sign new history after it. Keep the key in OpenBao or Vault, verify with a public key kept elsewhere, and keep an anchor on write-once storage. See the threat model. What guardrails do not inspect. Streamed tool-call arguments cannot be masked, so a guarded stream that carries them is stopped (ask without stream). Reasoning text, refusals, log probabilities and unknown fields are removed from guarded answers, not inspected. A secret whose start appears more than 256 bytes before it can match is not seen in a stream, and a span still open after 64 KiB is released masked only as far as it has reached. Guardrail audit entries are written asynchronously and dropped, counted and alerted when the queue is full. A Responses stream under post-call guardrails is refused. Phone numbers have no checksum: a PII guardrail that masks them also masks 10-digit references that start with 0. The performance of v0.6 and v0.7 is not measured yet. The overhead figures are those of v0.1.0; an independent benchmark of the current release is waiting for a quiet machine. The PDF export links more than it uses. Fixed in v0.15.2. go-pdfkit v0.20.0 moved its widget bridge to the subpackage pdfkit/widget, so the gateway no longer links go-widgets/toolkit and the code behind it. The binary went from 42,110,114 to 39,790,834 bytes, 5.5 % smaller (darwin/arm64, CGO_ENABLED=0 -trimpath, the same tree but for the bump; the README’s measurement on that commit). The library is documented at go-pdfkit.
data.mcp#MCP gateway:
POST /mcp is an MCP server in front of the tool servers of the configuration. It speaks the Streamable HTTP binding of revision 2026-07-28 and, for older clients, the initialize handshake of 2025-11-25 (and 2025-06-18, 2025-03-26). A client authenticates with its virtual key. This block passes llmflow-gateway check-config v0.16.1 (with the key files present, and an sso block, organisations, a pool and a model around it):
mcp_server "github" { url = "https://mcp.example.org/github/mcp" token_file = "/etc/llmflow/mcp-github.token" protocol = "2026-07-28" timeout = "60s" max_response_bytes = 8388608 } Tools are named .. Per-team allow-lists, closed by default. A team with no list sees no tool. An organisation administrator sets it with PUT /admin/teams/{team}/tools {"tools":["github.*","docs.search"]} (a pattern is *, .* or ., and must name a configured server). Team administrators can read the list but cannot widen it. A call to any other tool answers -32602 Unknown tool, like a tool that does not exist, and the refusal is audited (tool.denied). Every call is audited before it is made. A tool.call entry names the key, its organisation, team and project, the tool, and the SHA-256 and size of the arguments; the arguments are hashed, never stored. If that entry cannot be written, the call is not made (503). A tool.result entry follows with the outcome. llmflow_tool_calls_total{team,server,status} counts the calls, and the audit retention accepts the kind tool. Only configured servers are reached. Clients name tools, never URLs; the gateway sends requests only to the url of an mcp_server block, follows no redirect, uses no environment proxy and never fetches what a server returns. The tool servers’ tokens come from the secret source and the client’s key is never forwarded. Tool calls count against the key’s RPM and in-flight limits and cost no GPU-hours. Not covered: OAuth 2.1 discovery (virtual keys are static bearer tokens), resources and prompts, guardrails on tool arguments and results, and SSE toward MCP clients.
data.messages#Anthropic Messages API:
POST /v1/messages is proxied to vLLM’s own Anthropic endpoint, with no translation in the gateway, so coding agents that speak the Messages API can use local models. A virtual key is the bearer token. Guardrails cover system, text and thinking blocks, tool_result content and every string inside tool_use inputs; blocks they cannot read (a document) are refused. Guarded streams pass through an Anthropic event filter. Errors carry both OpenAI’s {"error": ...} and Anthropic’s top-level "type": "error".
/v1/messages/count_tokens (since v0.12.1) goes to vLLM’s own endpoint, which renders the chat template and counts the prompt’s tokens, so the count is exact ({"input_tokens": N}). Claude Code calls it, and falls back to a character-based estimate without it. It is authenticated, allow-listed and rate limited like /tokenize; it is not charged and not guarded. cache_salt and the engine fields are stripped, and chat_template_kwargs is kept, so the count matches the /v1/messages request that carries the same fields.
data.more-endpoints#More endpoints: All of these go through the same pipeline as chat: authentication, policies, budgets, rate limits, guardrails, fair-share priority and the tenant’s cache_salt.
data.overhead#Overhead:
An independent A/B against LiteLLM, measured on 2026-10-23.
Protocol. A Go tool, gwbench, with tests; its control test sees a planted 3 ms delay. Requests go one at a time, the order of the targets is randomised at every round, and the overhead is paired round by round against a direct call to the same fake upstream.
Targets. LiteLLM 1.106.2 (one process, no database) and llmflow v0.1.0 (GOMAXPROCS=1, memory store), on a small non-streaming request.
Load. Each run of 2,000 rounds starts only at a 1-minute load of 4 or less, and is discarded if the load ends above 4. A first long run was discarded (the load rose to 9.44). Eight runs were kept, at loads 3.30 to 3.94.
Result, over 16,000 paired rounds:
Overhead p50 p90 p99 LiteLLM 4.86 ms 5.26 ms 6.21 ms llmflow 117 us 161 us 239 us That is about 40 times lower at the median and 26 times at p99. The per-run median varied from 4.84 to 4.93 ms for LiteLLM and from 115 to 120 us for llmflow.
What it does not measure. No streaming, no concurrency, and no database write: the gateway ran with its memory store. These are to be measured on the cluster.
data.prefix-cache-isolation#Prefix-cache isol:
Why. vLLM reuses cached KV blocks across requests that share a prompt prefix. That reuse is a timing side channel: a caller can test whether a guessed prefix is already cached by measuring the time to first token, and so learn what another tenant sent. vLLM’s security guide documents it, and it is tracked as CVE-2025-46570. On a cluster shared by several institutions this is a leak between institutions.
What the gateway does. It removes any cache_salt the client sends and always sets its own: base64url(HMAC-SHA256(key, scope)), 43 characters (256 bits). The key is read from cache_salt_key_file, and the scope is set by cache_isolation:
cache_isolation One prefix cache per org (default) organisation (institution) team team key virtual key none nothing: a single tenant vLLM mixes the salt into the hash of the first KV block and every later block chains from it, so different scopes never share cached blocks. The salt is stable per scope (a random salt per request would disable prefix caching). Multimodal uuid values in the message content parts are rewritten per tenant, not stripped: a client can keep referring to media it sent earlier, while the same uuid sent by two tenants names two different cache entries.
Operating it. cache_salt_key_file must hold at least 32 random bytes and be readable by its owner only (mode 0600); it is mandatory unless cache_isolation = "none". Rotating the key means a cold prefix cache for everyone.
Residual risk. Within one scope the cache is shared. With the default org, users of the same institution can still probe each other by timing; team or key narrow that, at the cost of less cache reuse. And vLLM itself states that cache_salt is not an isolation boundary: tenants that need hard isolation need a vLLM instance of their own.
data.rerank#Rerank, tokenization, audio: POST /v1/rerank and /v2/rerank serve score models; they are guarded and charged on the usage’s prompt tokens. POST /tokenize and /detokenize are authenticated and rate limited but not charged and not guarded: no model runs, and masking would make the count wrong. POST /v1/audio/transcriptions takes a bounded multipart form, rebuilt from an allow-list of fields before it is forwarded. The file is limited by limits { max_audio_bytes } (25 MiB by default), and a model is charged with cost { audio_per_hour } in GPU-hours per hour of audio. The audio itself is not inspected, and the content log never holds it. A client chat_template is stripped from every request.
data.responses#Responses API: stateless only:
POST /v1/responses is proxied to vLLM’s own Responses endpoint. The gateway forces "store": false and refuses previous_response_id, background, conversation and a stored prompt with a 400 that says so. GET /v1/responses/{id} and the cancel route are not routed. Clients send the whole conversation in input, as with chat completions.
Why. vLLM can keep responses in the memory of the instance that produced them: it does so only when started with VLLM_ENABLE_RESPONSES_API_STORE=1. With that on, anyone holding an id could read a response back, continue it or cancel it, and behind a gateway that state would be shared by every tenant. The gateway forces store: false and refuses the stateful fields regardless, so a deployment with the store enabled stays safe. Verified against a real vLLM (see Benchmarking): GET /v1/responses/{id} through the gateway answers 404.
Usage is read from the Responses usage, including the final response.completed event of a stream. Guardrails read instructions and the input items; input items they cannot read are refused. A streamed Responses request under post-call guardrails is refused (400; ask with "stream": false).
data.roadmap#Roadmap:
Issue #7 tracks shipping every LiteLLM Enterprise feature in the open-source gateway. M1 (governance and multi-tenancy) is done, in v0.2.0, M2 (identity and access) in v0.4.0, and M3 (audit and logging) in v0.5.0, and M4 (guardrails) in v0.6.0. The version numbers written in the issue shifted by one when v0.3.0 was taken by the security patch.
A further milestone, issue #38 (“M5”), covers more endpoints and operations. Its first five items shipped in v0.7.0 (the endpoints, fallbacks and tracing described above), and the last two, the admin web UI and the MCP gateway, in v0.8.0. Issue #38 is closed and M5 is complete.
data.routes#Routes: Client routes: POST /v1/chat/completions, /v1/completions, /v1/embeddings, /v1/responses (stateless only), /v1/messages (Anthropic Messages API), /v1/rerank, /v2/rerank, /v1/audio/transcriptions, /tokenize, /detokenize, and GET /v1/models. Also GET /healthz, which returns 503 when the budget state is stale and fail-closed is on, and GET /metrics (Prometheus text format, optional bearer token). All are described under More endpoints; how coding agents use them is on the Coding agents page.
data.security#Security: Clients cannot choose their priority. The body is parsed and re-encoded (duplicate keys and escaped spellings cannot survive); priority, extra_body, request_id, kv_transfer_params, ec_transfer_params and vllm_xargs are removed. Upstream headers are built from scratch, so a client’s X-Vllm-Priority, x-pass-*, Authorization and X-Forwarded-* never reach vLLM. This closes a hole measured on LiteLLM. The rewrite and the SSE copier are fuzzed (FuzzRewrite, FuzzCopySSE). vLLM must only be reachable from the gateway. Its --api-key covers only /v1, /v2 and /inference; /invocations exposes inference without authentication. Firewall the vLLM ports (guide). Identity (v0.4.0). OpenID Connect access tokens are verified by go-authn/oidc (no alg: none, no HMAC, aud and exp required, https key fetches rate-limited), administrator sessions use a __Host- cookie with CSRF token and Origin check, and every refusal on the inference API is the same 401. X-Forwarded-For is read from the right and only from trusted_proxies; routes can be restricted to networks; IP allowlists must all match. Details on the Identity page. Audit (v0.5.0). Admin actions are in a hash-chained log with signed checkpoints, which an anchor on write-once storage makes hard to rewrite. What stays open is stated on the Audit and logging page. Keys. Virtual keys and admin tokens are 256-bit random secrets, stored as SHA-256, compared in constant time and shown once. Secrets come from files only and never appear in logs, errors or listings. No SSRF. Upstreams come from the configuration only; client input selects a model group, never a URL. Upstream redirects are not followed. Brute force. Failed authentications are limited per client network (IPv4 address or IPv6 /64, from the connection, not from proxy headers) by auth_failures_per_minute; valid and missed keys live in two separate bounded caches, so a spray of random keys cannot evict valid ones. Limits on body, headers, timeouts, request duration and upstream response size; a bounded accounting queue. Budgets fail closed: when PostgreSQL cannot be read for 3 refresh periods, every request gets 503 (fail_closed = false to fail open). CI: race tests on amd64 and arm64, PostgreSQL integration tests, fuzz smoke, govulncheck, CGO_ENABLED=0 cross-builds.
data.slurm-discovery#Slurm discovery: vLLM in:
A model can take its upstreams from Slurm instead of, or on top of, static upstream blocks. This is the slurm block inside a model block; the top-level slurm block of Finance reports is a different thing (the input of the reconciliation). The vLLM instances run as long jobs of a service account, for example account svc_llm with a QOS service, and can be stopped at night so that the GPUs can be lent to a borrowing QOS. The gateway follows the running jobs; it never starts or stops one. Slurm (scrontab) or the operator does that.
pool "gpu" { capacity = 0 } # 0: C is the sum of the instances' capacities model "llama" { upstream_model = "meta/llama-3.3-70b" pool = "gpu" key_file = "/etc/llmflow/vllm.key" # the instances' API key slurm { url = "https://slurmrestd.cluster:6820" # from here only api_version = "v0.0.44" # slurmrestd -d list token_file = "/etc/llmflow/slurm.jwt" # any secret reference user_name = "svc_llm" # X-SLURM-USER-NAME (optional) accounts = ["svc_llm"] # required partitions = ["gpu"] # required users = ["svc_llm"] # optional allow-list interval = "15s" stale_after = "5m" instance_capacity = 8 # when the job does not say max_instance_capacity = 64 } } This block passes llmflow-gateway check-config v0.16.1 (with the key files present, and organisations around it).
Convention. A job serves model M on port P when its name (or else its comment) is llmflow:M:P or llmflow:M:P:C. C is the instance’s contribution to the pool’s capacity; without it, instance_capacity applies. Discovery. Every interval the gateway reads GET /slurm//jobs/ with X-SLURM-USER-TOKEN. It keeps the jobs that are RUNNING and carry none of the COMPLETING, CONFIGURING, STOPPED, SIGNALING, RESIZING or REQUEUED flags, in an allowed account and partition (and user, when users is set). An instance is added only after GET /health answers 200 and GET /v1/models lists upstream_model. Removal. When the job leaves the list, or fails health 3 polls in a row, the instance is drained: no new request, not even as a last resort. It is removed once its requests in flight have finished, or after limits.max_request_duration. Capacity. The pool’s C is its configured capacity plus the capacities of its non-draining instances. Every membership change re-apportions the organisations' integer reservations with the same Hamilton method, and is audited (slurm.member_added, slurm.member_drained, slurm.member_removed, pool.capacity). Requests in flight keep their status. Safety. Only the configured accounts, partitions and users are trusted: without that, anyone could submit a job named llmflow:llama:8000 and capture prompts. An untrusted job claiming a model is logged once and counted in llmflow_slurm_rejected_jobs_total{reason}. The URL comes from the configuration only; batch_host must be a plain host name; the JWT is a secret reference and is never sent across a redirect (redirects are refused); the answer is bounded to 32 MiB and 100,000 jobs. Fail-closed. While slurmrestd cannot be read, the last known members are kept and still health-checked. Past stale_after the gateway logs an error and admits no instance until a poll succeeds. Healthy members are never dropped because of an outage. Metrics. llmflow_pool_capacity, llmflow_slurm_polls_total{outcome}, llmflow_slurm_last_success_timestamp_seconds, llmflow_slurm_rejected_jobs_total. With an ha block (since v0.15.2). Every replica runs its own discovery and health checks, for its own routing: publishing the healthy set through PostgreSQL was not chosen, because it would tie every replica’s routing to the owner’s liveness and to PostgreSQL, and because what is healthy depends on a replica’s network path to the instance. Only the pool’s owner’s view sets C. It decides with it and publishes C and the integer reservations with the lease’s epoch (llmflow_pool_capacity shows the decided C on every replica); a replica that sees fewer instances still routes only to those it sees. A replica takes a pool only after its discovery has read the members once; until then requests are admitted at the lowest priority (or refused under on_owner_unreachable = "reject"). An owner whose slurmrestd stays unreadable past stale_after yields: a replica that still reads the jobs takes the lease (epoch + 1) and stays quiet for one lease_ttl, until the previous owner’s validity has surely ended. If no replica reads slurmrestd, the owner keeps the pool with its last known members. Chaos tests with a real PostgreSQL: the owner killed while a job joins (the survivor owns with the new C at epoch + 1); slurmrestd lost by the owner only (handover after 1.2 s, never two owners in about 950 samples, and the test fails without the quiet period); two replicas that disagree (each routes to what it sees, the fair share is the owner’s). The sum of the reservations never exceeded C in any sample. The token is read at start only. Issue it with scontrol token username=svc_llm lifespan=... and pick a lifespan longer than your restart cycle: the default is 1800 s. Once it has expired, polls fail and the fail-closed rule applies. slurmrestd needs AuthAltTypes=auth/jwt. An instance as a job, from the README’s template (the key is read into VLLM_API_KEY, never passed with --api-key, because the node’s process list shows every command line to every user):
#!/bin/bash #SBATCH --job-name=llmflow:llama:8000:8 #SBATCH --account=svc_llm --qos=service --partition=gpu #SBATCH --nodes=1 --gres=gpu:4 --exclusive --time=7-00:00:00 #SBATCH --signal=B:TERM@120 VLLM_API_KEY=$(cat /etc/llmflow/vllm.key); export VLLM_API_KEY exec vllm serve meta/llama-3.3-70b --served-model-name meta/llama-3.3-70b \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --tensor-parallel-size 4 The node’s vLLM port must be reachable by the gateway only (firewall): /metrics is unauthenticated and the key protects /v1 only.
Day and night with scrontab (needs ScronParameters=enable):
#SCRON --account=svc_llm --qos=service --partition=service -t 0:05:00 0 7 * * 1-5 sbatch /opt/llmflow/vllm-llama.sbatch #SCRON --account=svc_llm --qos=service --partition=service -t 0:05:00 0 20 * * 1-5 scancel --account=svc_llm --name=llmflow:llama:8000:8 At 20:00 the jobs end, the gateway drains them, its pool shrinks and the reservations follow. At 07:00 the new jobs are admitted as soon as vLLM answers.
Tested against a real Slurm (bench TestSlurmDiscoveryE2E, 2026-10-26, Slurm 24.11.5, slurmrestd data_parser v0.0.42, arm64, a vLLM CPU job serving Qwen2.5-0.5B): admitted 18 s after sbatch, a chat request answered 200, removed 2 s after scancel; a job of another account claiming the model was rejected and never contacted; a vLLM job whose engine failed to start stayed RUNNING and was never admitted. See Benchmarking. That is one small instance on one node, not a production cluster.

data.upgrading-v0100#Upgrading to v0.10.0:
store.spool_dir is mandatory with the postgres store: without it the gateway refuses to start. It is the directory of the durable accounting spool: every batch of usage records is appended to a file there and fsync’d before it is inserted, so that records survive a PostgreSQL outage or a crash, within the bounds listed under Limitations (the gateway’s README, “Durable accounting”). The directory is created with mode 0700 and refused if group- or world-writable; files are mode 0600. store.spool_max_bytes caps it (256 MiB per process by default). Metrics: llmflow_accounting_spooled, llmflow_accounting_replayed_total; alert accounting_records_lost. A process that dies leaves its file, and the next process on the directory adopts and stores it. Also new: sso.min_refresh (at least 5 s, as for jwt).
store { kind = "postgres" dsn_file = "/etc/llmflow/pg.dsn" spool_dir = "/var/lib/llmflow/spool" spool_max_bytes = 268435456 }

data.fair-share#Fair-share on a co-owned GPU:
How to share four HGX B300 servers (32 GPUs) between two institutions, A and B, with Slurm for batch computing, vLLM for inference, a gateway for keys and quotas, and VS Code to reach it all. The sharing must respect each institution’s share and leave no GPU idle.
This is an English adaptation of a design and operations document, version 1.1 of 23 October 2026. Every parameter cited refers to the vendors’ documentation consulted on that date (see the bibliography). The measurements are real and dated: they were made on LiteLLM 1.106.2 on 23 October 2026.
The guide has three layers, one page each:
Slurm guarantees each institution its share (QOS caps, preemption of borrowing jobs) and divides the rest by fair-share (the Fair Tree algorithm): Slurm. vLLM serves the language models in long Slurm jobs, and a gateway in front of it authenticates users, applies per-institution quotas and counts consumption in tokens: Inference. One accounting, in GPU-hours, ties the two: Accounting. Then VS Code access, identity with your federation (RENATER, eduGAIN), the security audit, acceptance tests and governance, and the bibliography.
data.hardware#The hardware:
Each server is an HGX B300 with 8 Blackwell Ultra SXM GPUs linked by NVLink 5. Figures are NVIDIA’s (the HGX datasheet, the Blackwell Ultra technical blog and the DGX B300 user guide).
per GPU per server (8 GPUs) HBM3e memory 288 GB 2.3 TB (8 x 288); 2.1 TB on the HGX datasheet HBM bandwidth 8 TB/s – NVLink 5, GPU to GPU (bidirectional) 1.8 TB/s 14.4 TB/s in total NVFP4, dense / sparse 15 / 20 PFLOPS 108 / 144 PFLOPS FP8, dense / sparse 5 / 10 PFLOPS 36 / 72 PFLOPS FP64 – 10 TFLOPS INT8 (sparse) – 3 POPS (72 on HGX B200) MIG partitions up to 7 instances (for example 7 x 34 GB) – Power TGP up to 1,400 W DGX B300: 14.5 kW, 15 kW max Per-GPU and per-server figures are not always in a ratio of 8: 108/8 = 13.5 PFLOPS rather than 15, and 2.1 TB rather than 8 x 288 GB. NVIDIA states that memory and SM count vary by part number. Use the values of your vendor’s datasheet. As an example, the DGX B300 has 2 Xeon Platinum 6776P and 2 TB of RAM (up to 4).
The B300 is an AI machine, not a double-precision scientific one. 10 TFLOPS of FP64 for 8 GPUs, and an INT8 rate divided by 24 relative to the B200. A classic FP64 code (CFD, quantum chemistry, finite elements) wastes its institution’s share here. The agreement between the institutions should say so; such codes belong on other facilities. The cluster has 32 GPUs. A practical consequence: a model served with tensor parallelism 8 (--tensor-parallel-size 8) occupies a whole server, because NVLink does not connect two servers.
data.hybrid#The hybrid model in one sentence:
By default each institution submits to its own owner QOS, capped at its share; those jobs are never preempted. Beyond its share it submits to the borrow QOS, uncapped but preemptible by the owner QOS. Among waiting jobs, the order depends on fair-share, which penalises the institution that consumed more than its share over the last two weeks.
VS Code ──HTTPS──> gateway (keys, teams, quotas, accounting) ──internal──> vLLM (Continue, (Slurm jobs, Remote-SSH) QOS service) └──SSH──> login node (sbatch, srun) ──> slurmctld + slurmdbd ──> gpu01 ... gpu04 (Fair Tree, QOS, preemption) 4 x 8 B300
data.objectives#Objectives: Guarantee: each institution gets its share (26 or 6 GPUs) within a bounded, known delay, even when the cluster is full. No loss: a GPU its owner does not use is lent to the other institution. Fairness over time: over a sliding window, each one’s consumption tends to its share. Whoever borrowed a lot goes behind the other. One accounting: batch and inference are both read in GPU-hours, for re-invoicing and governance. Security: GPU isolation between jobs, and no inference service reachable without authentication.

Institution A bought 3 whole servers and the remaining quarter of the 4th; institution B bought the other three quarters of the 4th. If a later purchase changes the split, update this table and the values derived from it (Fairshare, GrpTRES).

data.accounting#One accounting:
Batch is counted in GPU-equivalent hours (sreport, after TRESBillingWeights). Inference is counted in tokens, per team (the gateway’s spend logs). They are reconciled as follows:
Over the period (a month), read the GPU-hours of the svc_llm account: H_svc. Read each team’s spend in the gateway: D_A, D_B. Charge H_svc x D_A / (D_A + D_B) to A, and the remainder to B. Compare each institution’s total consumption (batch plus charged inference) with its share (81.25 % / 18.75 %).
data.calibration#Calibrating the internal cos:
Goal: 1 unit of gateway spend = 1 GPU-hour. A saturated 8-GPU instance then “spends” 8 units per hour, and max_budget becomes a quota of inference GPU-hours, directly comparable with batch.
1. Measure the capacity. Once per model and per configuration (TP, KV-cache dtype), with vllm bench serve [24]. Use a mix of lengths representative of the real usage (for example 2,000 input tokens and 300 output tokens for a code assistant). Raise --max-concurrency up to the limit of the service target, for instance a p99 time to first token under 2 s:
vllm bench serve --backend openai-chat --endpoint /v1/chat/completions \ --host gpu01.internal --port 8000 --model \ --dataset-name random --random-input-len 2000 --random-output-len 300 \ --num-prompts 2000 --max-concurrency 64 --save-result At the chosen concurrency C (which also serves the fair-share relay), read the output throughput T_out and the total throughput T_tot in tokens/s, printed by the tool [24]. The input throughput is T_in = T_tot - T_out.
2. Split the cost of an instance-hour. Prefill (input) costs much less per token than generation. Fix a ratio r = c_out / c_in, typically r = 4, and solve:
3600 (c_in T_in + c_out T_out) = 8 => c_in = 8 / (3600 (T_in + r T_out)), c_out = r c_in A fictitious example, to illustrate the computation (the real figures come out of step 1): T_in = 40,000, T_out = 6,000 tokens/s, r = 4. Then c_in = 8 / (3600 x 64,000) = 3.5e-8 and c_out = 1.4e-7 unit per token.
3. Tokens served from the prefix cache. LiteLLM warns that a model with custom pricing bills these tokens at 0 as long as cache_read_input_token_cost is not set (a warning observed at LiteLLM 1.106.2 start-up). Set it to about c_in / 10: these tokens are not recomputed, but they occupy KV memory.
Why not a cost per second? LiteLLM accepts cost_per_second [22]. But vLLM processes dozens of requests simultaneously on one instance: billing each by its duration would make it pay for the whole instance, and the sum would far exceed the real 8 GPU-hours. The per-token cost is the right model.
Recalibrate at each change of model, vLLM version or KV-cache dtype, and check once a month. The GPU-hours of the svc_llm account read from sreport should stay close to the month’s total gateway spend divided by the average occupancy.
data.compensation#Compensation: If, over a quarter, an institution consumed markedly more than its share through inference, the committee may correct the Slurm Fairshare values of the next quarter. Batch fair-share already rebalances by itself within the half-life window: compensation is only an exceptional adjustment.

data.acceptance#Acceptance tests: prove the g:
Every guarantee is proven by a test that could fail:
B’s guarantee. A fills the 32 GPUs (13 in instA, 19 in borrow). B submits 3 GPUs in instB. Measure the start delay: it must stay under 36 minutes, and under 6 minutes if the borrowed jobs are older than 30 minutes. Negative control. The same scenario with the borrow QOS without Preempt: B must wait. If B starts anyway, test 1 was not measuring preemption. Cap. B submits 8 GPUs in instB: immediate rejection (DenyOnLimit). Fair-share. After a week in which B borrows heavily, sshare -l must show LF_B < 1, and A’s borrow jobs must go ahead of B’s (sprio). Billing. A job of 1 GPU and 64 cores must be billed 4: the billing= field of AllocTRES in sacct. Inference. Saturate the model with a key of A; check that a key of B still gets about 18.75 % of the throughput (with the Enterprise reservation, or the relay) or its static limit. vLLM priority. During saturation, a request of the large-model group (priority 0) must have a time to first token markedly lower than a request of large-model-batch (priority 10). Inviolable priority. Send to large-model-batch a request with extra_body: {"priority": 0} and a header X-Vllm-Priority: 0. It must stay processed at priority 10. Control: the same request sent directly to vLLM goes ahead. B’s window. One hour before instB_weekly opens, submit in borrow a 3 h job and a 30 min job. Only the second must start on the reserved server. At opening, an 8-GPU job of B must start immediately. Performance. Compare throughput (tokens/s) and latency (time to first token, p50/p99) of vLLM behind the gateway with those of vLLM direct, at equal load. The gateway’s overhead must stay negligible next to generation; if it does not, increase the number of gateway workers before touching vLLM.
data.governance#Governance: Agreement between institutions: shares (26/6), guaranteed delay (36 min), size of the inference pool, half-life (14 days), the quarterly compensation rule, and the possible reservation of a whole server for B. Quarterly technical committee: real consumption against share, median wait times per institution and per QOS, preemption rate, inference saturation. Change of shares (the purchase of a 5th server, say): change the Fairshare and GrpTRES values. No redeployment is needed.
data.security-audit#Security audit:
Surface Risk Measure Shared GPUs a job reads the GPU memory of another institution ConstrainDevices=yes [7]; no shard between institutions [5] vLLM unauthenticated endpoints outside /v1 [10] internal listening only; firewall: only the gateway reaches it Gateway quota bypass during a Redis/DB outage [11] fail-closed options; Redis and Postgres made redundant Gateway budgets inoperative on a zero-cost model [11] non-zero internal cost (accounting) Keys leak through a URL, a command line or an environment variable files with mode 0600; Continue secrets; rotation; one key per use Logs confidential prompts stored in the database disable message-content logging; keep only spend metadata vLLM prefix cache timing side channel between institutions: a caller detects a cached prefix by its time to first token (CVE-2025-46570) per-tenant cache_salt set by the gateway (prefix-cache isolation); a vLLM instance per tenant if hard isolation is needed Login node computation outside Slurm per-user cgroup limits; SSH access to GPU nodes reserved to jobs Preemption loss of work of borrowed jobs GraceTime plus checkpoint; PreemptExemptTime vLLM priority a client gives itself priority 0 through extra_body (measured, measurements) priority pinned by header; client-header forwarding disabled; the relay (or the Go gateway) overwrites Header forwarding the client’s x-pass-* and x-* reach vLLM if forwarding is on [23] leave forward_client_headers_to_llm_api disabled FP64 usage double-precision codes on B300 (10 TFLOPS per server) [12] usage rule in the agreement Audit anchor. The Go gateway (audit log since v0.5.0) keeps a hash-chained audit log of every administrative change, with signed checkpoints. A log in the database that the operator can edit is only partly trustworthy: deploy the audit anchor on the same S3 or Ceph storage the cluster already has, in a bucket created with Object Lock, so that exported checkpoints cannot be deleted or rewritten, and check the log with llmflow-gateway audit verify --anchor export and a public key kept outside the operators’ reach. Without an anchor, truncation and rollback go undetected. The Audit and logging page states what remains open.
Guardrails (gateway v0.6.0). Prompts and completions can be checked before and after vLLM, on this cluster, without sending them anywhere: hide_secrets masks tokens and URL credentials (using gitsafe’s redact), pii masks or blocks personal data (e-mail, phone, IBAN, French NIR, cards, IP addresses) with go-llmflow/pii, and llama_guard and prompt_guard classify with a Llama Guard or Prompt Guard model served locally by vLLM on the cluster, as a model of class guard that clients cannot call. The classifiers see the already-masked text. A guardrail that errs or times out refuses (503) by default. The generic HTTP adapter is off by default: it exists only when written, and then only with allow_external = true, because it sends prompts and completions out of the site. This block passes check-config v0.16.1:
guardrail "secrets" { type = "hide_secrets" orgs = ["instA", "instB"] } guardrail "pii" { type = "pii" teams = ["b-lab"] action = "mask" actions = { iban = "block", nir = "block", phone = "log" } } guardrail "safety" { type = "llama_guard" model = "llama-guard" teams = ["b-lab"] action = "block" timeout = "2s" on_error = "block" } model "llama-guard" { upstream_model = "meta-llama/Llama-Guard-3-8B" pool = "guard" class = "guard" key_file = "/etc/llmflow/vllm.key" upstream "g0" { base_url = "http://gpu09:8000" } } (Alongside the organisations, teams, the pool "guard" and the other models.)
Chaos to play during acceptance. Kill a vLLM instance under sustained traffic (the routing must fail over); cut Redis (the fail-closed mode must answer 503, not let requests through); preempt a borrowed job in the middle of writing a checkpoint (the resume must read the last complete checkpoint); restart slurmdbd during a mass submission.

data.bridge#1. Register the gateway at the br:
The gateway is a client of the bridge. This block is authn-bridge’s configuration, copied from the gateway’s README (it is not llmflow-gateway configuration, so check-config does not apply to it):
client "llmflow-admin" { secret_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/llmflow-admin.secret" redirect_uris = ["https://llm.example.org/admin/callback"] id_token_claims = true # the bridge's ID tokens carry no claims about the person otherwise }
data.gateway#2. Point the gateway’s sso and j:
Administrators log in through sso; users of the inference API present the access token through jwt. The groups the bridge returns are entitlements held to the institution that asserted them, so the role and map blocks match them. This block was run through llmflow-gateway check-config v0.16.1 (with the key files present, and organisations, a pool and a model alongside):
master_key_file = "/etc/llmflow/master.key" cache_salt_key_file = "/etc/llmflow/cache-salt.key" sso { issuer = "https://bridge.example.org" client_id = "llmflow-admin" client_secret_file = "/etc/llmflow/sso.secret" redirect_url = "https://llm.example.org/admin/callback" scopes = ["openid", "profile", "groups"] role { value = "llm-admins" role = "proxy_admin" } role { value = "b-lab-leads" role = "team_admin" team = "b-lab" } } jwt { issuer = "https://bridge.example.org" audience = "llmflow" type = "at+jwt" map { value = "b-lab" team = "b-lab" } } With this, a member of B’s laboratory who holds a token with the group b-lab reaches the gateway as a person of team b-lab: their requests count in B’s share, their budget and limits are the team’s, and the spend report names them. The value strings stand for whatever entitlements your federation really issues (for example urn:mace:... values); read them from a real token before writing the blocks.
Behind it, the gateway refuses alg: none and HMAC tokens, requires aud and exp, and answers every refusal with the same 401. See the Identity page for the details, for SCIM provisioning and for key rotation, and keep in mind its limitations: a person holding a token cannot be revoked individually before it expires, and SSO sessions live in one replica.
data.identity#Identity with your federation:
On a cluster co-owned by two institutions, people already have an account at their own institution. The aim is that nobody needs a second one: A’s and B’s users log in where they always do, and the gateway learns from that login which team they belong to.
If the institutions are in a SAML federation such as RENATER (France) or eduGAIN, the piece in the middle is authn-bridge (go-authn/bridge): an OpenID Connect provider placed in front of the federation. People log in at their own university; the gateway, which speaks OpenID Connect, gets a token. The bridge and the libraries below are documented in go-authn’s repositories; this page only shows how the gateway is pointed at them.
user ──> their university (SAML, RENATER / eduGAIN) │ v authn-bridge (OpenID Connect provider) │ token v llmflow gateway: sso (administrators), jwt (inference API) ──> vLLM

data.elastic-pool#Elastic pool: At night and at weekends interactive inference drops. An scontrol update or a scrontab can stop one instance in two: 8 GPUs go back to the borrow QOS, without changing A’s and B’s guarantees. On the gateway side the second instance leaves the routing; its requests go to the first, which stays available.
data.fair-share-inference#Fair-share for infe:
LiteLLM’s dynamic_rate_limiter_v3 shares a model’s TPM/RPM capacity between teams. Below a saturation threshold anyone may borrow the free capacity. Above it, each priority is brought back to its reserved share [14]. It is a direct transposition of the Slurm model: lending of surplus, guarantee at saturation.
litellm_settings: callbacks: ["dynamic_rate_limiter_v3"] priority_reservation: instA: 0.8125 instB: 0.1875 saturation_threshold: 0.8 A key’s priority comes from its team’s metadata.priority, which wins over the key’s. Keys with no priority fall into a common pool (default_priority, 0.25 by default) [14]. The model’s capacity (rpm/tpm of the deployments) is measured in acceptance on your B300s, at the target latency.
(1) Priority reservation is marked beta and requires a LiteLLM Enterprise licence (30-day free trial) [14]. (2) Borrowed capacity is not taken back when strict mode engages, and TPM is checked at admission: a burst can exceed the limit. (3) With several LiteLLM instances, strict mode may engage late on a node that has not seen the traffic (60 s cache by default) [14].
data.fairq#Split with lending, without a lice:
Free-edition LiteLLM provides keys, teams, budgets and static limits (tpm_limit, rpm_limit, max_parallel_requests) [11]. What is missing is the lending. Static limits at 81.25 / 18.75 leave an absent institution’s share unused.
The proposal is to reproduce the Slurm scheme (guaranteed share plus preemptible borrowing) at request level: a small relay between the gateway and vLLM counts the requests in flight per institution. Let C be the sustainable concurrency of an instance, measured (see accounting).
If the institution has fewer than p x C requests in flight (p = 0.8125 or 0.1875), the request is within its share: X-Vllm-Priority is 0 (interactive) or 1 (batch). Otherwise it is borrowing: priority 10 (interactive) or 11 (batch). The relay overwrites any priority and any X-Vllm-Priority coming from the client. vLLM then does exactly what is expected (see priority): within-share requests are admitted before borrowing ones; when KV memory runs short, borrowers are preempted first. Without competition an institution takes everything; under saturation each gets its share back.
This is the policy the gateway (v0.16.1) implements in its fairshare package, with the two refinements the simulator forced (the reservation test counts within-share requests, and usage is charged at release). It replaces LiteLLM and the relay here: it holds the keys, organisations, teams and budgets itself, and the shares belong to the organisations (the institutions). For this cluster, its configuration (HCL2, not YAML) would be as follows, with the 256-request capacity of the gateway’s example. This block was run through llmflow-gateway check-config v0.16.1, with the key files present:
master_key_file = "/etc/llmflow/master.key" cache_isolation = "org" cache_salt_key_file = "/etc/llmflow/cache-salt.key" org "instA" { share = 0.8125 team "a-physics" {} team "a-biology" {} } org "instB" { share = 0.1875 team "b-lab" {} } pool "b300" { capacity = 256 } model "large-model" { upstream_model = "meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct" pool = "b300" class = "interactive" key_file = "/etc/llmflow/vllm.key" cost { input_per_mtok = 0.02 output_per_mtok = 0.20 cached_per_mtok = 0.002 } upstream "gpu01" { base_url = "http://gpu01.internal:8000" } upstream "gpu02" { base_url = "http://gpu02.internal:8000" } } # the same upstreams again, with class = "batch" model "large-model-batch" { upstream_model = "meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct" pool = "b300" class = "batch" key_file = "/etc/llmflow/vllm.key" cost { input_per_mtok = 0.02 output_per_mtok = 0.20 cached_per_mtok = 0.002 } upstream "gpu01" { base_url = "http://gpu01.internal:8000" } upstream "gpu02" { base_url = "http://gpu02.internal:8000" } } The cost values are in GPU-hours per million tokens; calibrate them as in the accounting page. Note the gateway’s limitations, in particular one replica per pool.
To validate: how the relay knows the institution. Two routes. (a) One deployment per institution (api_base: http://relay:9000/instA/v1), reachable only by the team’s keys: safe, but one must check how LiteLLM exposes a single model name to two teams. (b) The X-Litellm-User_api_key_* headers that LiteLLM adds with add_user_information_to_llm_headers: we observed them (user id, key fingerprint). The presence of the team id could not be verified, because our test ran without a database, hence without teams.
data.inference#Inference: Shared inference is vLLM running inside Slurm, behind a gateway that is the only HTTPS entry point. In the original design the gateway is LiteLLM; the measurements below are of LiteLLM 1.106.2. The Go gateway of this organisation implements the fair-share policy that LiteLLM’s free edition lacks.
data.prefix-cache-isolation#Prefix-cache isol: With --enable-prefix-caching, vLLM reuses cached KV blocks across requests that share a prompt prefix. That reuse is a timing side channel between tenants: a caller can tell from the time to first token whether a guessed prefix was cached, hence whether another institution sent it (vLLM’s security guide; CVE-2025-46570). On a cluster shared by A and B this must be closed. The vLLM mechanism is the cache_salt request field, mixed into the hash of the first KV block. The Go gateway (v0.3.0) always sets a stable per-tenant salt (an HMAC of the tenant under a secret key file of at least 32 random bytes) and drops the client’s own; cache_isolation chooses the tenant (org by default, team, key, or none). Two limits to keep in mind: users inside one scope can still probe each other (team or key narrow it, at the cost of cache reuse), and cache_salt is not a hard isolation boundary, which only a vLLM instance per tenant is. Rotating the key empties everyone’s cache.
data.priority#Per-request priority:
A request may carry an integer priority: the lower it is, the sooner the request runs (default 0). The X-Vllm-Priority header takes precedence over the JSON body. Any non-zero value is an error if the server was not started with --scheduling-policy priority [10].
What the scheduler does, from its source code [25]:
the waiting queue is a heap sorted by (priority, arrival_time): the smallest priority comes out first, arrival breaks ties; when a running request cannot find KV-cache blocks any more, vLLM preempts the running request with the largest (priority, arrival_time) and puts it back at the head of the queue; a high-priority waiting request does not preempt a running request: it takes the first slot that frees up. Priority therefore orders admission and designates the victims when memory runs short. It does not interrupt generations in progress. Since a generation lasts a few seconds, the effect on latency is quick. We use it to put interactive use (VS Code, chat) ahead of API batch processing, and for the split between institutions (below).
data.routing#Models and routing:
This is LiteLLM’s configuration; the interactive group pins priority 0 and the batch group pins priority 10, on the same instances.

A failing deployment goes into cooldown alone, not the whole group [13].
Zero costs = budgets ignored. A model whose two costs are 0 is subject to no budget check [11]. The model is hosted locally, but it must still be given an internal cost, calibrated in GPU-hours (see accounting). Otherwise max_budget protects nothing. Costs are declared under model_info [22]. Measured on LiteLLM 1.106.2: without a cost, spend stays at 0; with a cost, it equals exactly 3 c_in + 1 c_out for 3 input tokens and 1 output token.
data.securing-vllm#Securing vLLM: --api-key protects only the /v1, /v2 and /inference paths. Other endpoints of the same server, such as /invocations, are not authenticated. The documentation asks not to rely on --api-key alone and to put vLLM behind a proxy [10]. Hence the rules: vLLM listens on the cluster’s internal interface only; a firewall lets only the gateway reach the vLLM ports; the internal key is read from a file, never passed in clear in the environment or in shell history.
data.teams-keys#Teams, keys and limits:
# One team per institution (indicative values) curl -X POST https://llm.example.org/team/new \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat ~/.config/litellm/master)" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"team_alias": "instA", "max_budget": 1300, "budget_duration": "30d", "max_parallel_requests": 200, "metadata": {"priority": "instA"}}' curl -X POST https://llm.example.org/team/new ... \ -d '{"team_alias": "instB", "max_budget": 300, "budget_duration": "30d", "max_parallel_requests": 50, "metadata": {"priority": "instB"}}' # One key per user, attached to their team curl -X POST https://llm.example.org/key/generate ... \ -d '{"team_id": "", "key_alias": "bob-vscode", "rpm_limit": 60, "max_parallel_requests": 8}' A key that carries a team_id is governed by the team’s budget, not by its owner’s personal budget. The limits tpm_limit, rpm_limit and max_parallel_requests can be set on the team, the user or the key. For one per-model limit, the key’s wins over the team’s [11]. The budget resets at each budget_duration [11].
Do not pass the secret on the command line. The examples read the master key from a file readable by its owner only, never from an environment variable or an argument visible in ps.
data.the-gateway#The gateway:
The gateway is the only HTTPS entry point of inference. It carries:
identity: a virtual key per user, attached to a team = an institution; quotas: rate (tokens/min, requests/min, concurrent requests) and a budget per team; the 81.25 / 18.75 split under saturation; accounting: spend in tokens per team, the basis of the re-charging. With LiteLLM, budgets are enforced only with a Postgres database. Without one they are not enforced at all [11]. With several LiteLLM instances Redis is needed too, or each instance counts on its own and limits can be exceeded. Enable fail_closed_budget_enforcement and fail_closed_rate_limit_enforcement: if Redis or the database fails, the gateway answers 503 instead of letting requests through uncounted [11].
data.vllm-in-slurm#vLLM in Slurm:
Each vLLM instance is a long Slurm job in the svc_llm account and the service QOS. It is therefore accounted, cgroup-isolated, and never preempted. For a whole server:

data.what-litellm-forwards#What LiteLLM forwa:
The documentation does not say what reaches vLLM. We measured it on 23 October 2026. A real LiteLLM 1.106.2 was placed in front of a fake vLLM written in Go that records every request it receives: path, headers, JSON body. Control: a request sent directly to the fake vLLM with priority: 99 and the header X-Vllm-Priority: 99 shows up intact. So the instrument does see what it looks for.
Sent by the client to LiteLLM Received by vLLM "priority": 10 in the body nothing: LiteLLM consumes this field for its own beta scheduler [15] (response header x-litellm-request-prioritization-used, +300 ms latency) "extra_body": {"priority": 3} "priority": 3 in the body deployment extra_body: {priority: 5} + client extra_body at 0 "priority": 0: the client overrides the deployment’s value deployment extra_headers: {X-Vllm-Priority: "6"} X-Vllm-Priority: 6 same + client X-Vllm-Priority: 0, client headers forwarded [23] X-Vllm-Priority: "0, 6": values merged, no longer an integer same + client X-Vllm-Priority: 0 and x-pass-X-Vllm-Priority: 1, default settings X-Vllm-Priority: 6: the client’s headers do not pass Conclusion: the only safe configuration.
Pin the priority by header in the deployment (extra_headers), never by extra_body. Leave forward_client_headers_to_llm_api disabled (the default). A client can still slip priority into the body through extra_body. But vLLM gives the header precedence over the body [10], so the pinned header wins. Do not use LiteLLM’s own priority field: it enables a beta scheduler that adds latency. The class of service (interactive or batch) is then chosen by the model name (large-model or large-model-batch). The keys of batch scripts are restricted to the second.

data.billing#Measuring consumption: GPU billi:
By default consumption is measured in CPU x seconds [2]. On a GPU cluster that is wrong: a job taking 1 core and 8 GPUs would cost almost nothing. So TRESBillingWeights is set on the partition [2], with PriorityFlags=MAX_TRES. A job’s billing then becomes the per-node maximum of the weighted TRES (CPU, memory, GRES) [2], not their sum.
The weights are calibrated so that a whole server is worth 8 units, whichever resource saturates it. For a server of C cores and M GiB of allocatable memory:
w_GPU = 1 w_CPU = 8 / C w_Mem = 8 / M With C = 128 and M = 3072 GiB: CPU=0.0625,Mem=0.0026G,GRES/gpu=1.0. A job taking 1 GPU but 64 cores is billed 4 units, because it makes 4 GPUs unusable for others. The unit of account becomes the GPU-equivalent second.
To validate: replace C and M by the values of slurmd -C [5] on your servers (CPUs and RealMemory minus the memory reserved for the system).
data.decay#Decay of consumption: PriorityDecayHalfLife is 7 days by default and applies every PriorityCalcPeriod (5 minutes by default) [2]. We recommend 14 days: training jobs on B300 often last several days, and a too-short half-life would erase a consumption debt before the other institution could catch up. PriorityUsageResetPeriod stays NONE: an abrupt reset creates edge effects at the start of a period.
data.fair-tree#The Fair Tree algorithm:
Fair Tree has been Slurm’s default since 19.05 [2]. At each level of the association tree it computes the Level Fairshare [1]:
LF = S / U S = S_self / S_(self+siblings) U = U_self / U_(self+siblings) LF > 1 means under-served; LF < 1, over-served; LF = infinity with no consumption. Siblings are sorted by decreasing LF, the tree is walked depth first, and each user receives a rank. The user’s fair-share factor is rank / number of users: 1.0 for the first [1].
The decisive property for us: the first level compares A against B before looking at users. If A is over-served, all of B’s users come before all of A’s, whatever individual consumption is. This is exactly the wanted behaviour between two institutions.
A worked example. Over the last 14 days (with decay), A consumed 70 % of the billed GPU-hours and B 30 %:
LF_A = 0.8125 / 0.70 = 1.16 LF_B = 0.1875 / 0.30 = 0.625 A is under-served relative to its share, so it goes first: its users get the highest ranks. B’s borrowing jobs will wait until A’s usage is back to normal. B’s jobs in its owner QOS remain guaranteed (see QOS).
data.gres-cgroup#gres.conf and cgroup.conf:
# gres.conf -- automatic detection through NVML AutoDetect=nvml # cgroup.conf ConstrainCores=yes ConstrainDevices=yes ConstrainRAMSpace=yes With AutoDetect=nvml, Slurm fills in the details of detected GPUs. The Gres= line of slurm.conf stays mandatory, and a node exposing fewer GPUs than announced goes to DRAIN [5].
ConstrainDevices=yes limits a job to the devices of its GRES allocation [7]. Without it a job could open another institution’s GPUs.
MIG (optional). For small inference or TP jobs, the B300s can be cut into MIG instances. Slurm manages them with AutoDetect=nvml on the nodes concerned, each instance typed by its profile [5]. Shards, on the other hand, do not partition processes on the GPU [5]: reserve them for uses inside one institution.
data.monitoring#Monitoring: Command What it shows sshare -l each association’s Level FS [1]: are A and B over- or under-served? sprio -l decomposition of the priority of waiting jobs by factor sreport cluster AccountUtilizationByUser -T gres/gpu GPU-hours per account over a period scontrol show job the PreemptEligibleTime [3] of a borrowed job
data.multifactor#Multifactor priority: With PriorityType=priority/multifactor, a job’s priority is an integer: a site factor, plus the sum of each factor (age, association, fair-share, size, partition, QOS, TRES) times its weight, minus the nice value. Each factor is between 0 and 1 and weights default to 0, so only the configured factors count [2].
data.preemption#Preemption:
PreemptType=preempt/qos: the rules come from the QOS in the database [3]. PreemptMode=REQUEUE: the preempted job is put back in the queue. This requires JobRequeue=1 or sbatch --requeue [3]. SUSPEND is rejected: a suspended job keeps its memory, hence its 288 GB of HBM per GPU, and the owner QOS would recover nothing [3]. PreemptExemptTime: minimum run time before being preemptible [3]. We choose 30 min, so that a borrowed job makes at least some progress. GraceTime on the borrow QOS: the delay between SIGTERM and SIGKILL [3], used to write a checkpoint. We choose 300 s. Guaranteed delay. An owner job that fits in its QOS starts after at most
PreemptExemptTime + GraceTime + one scheduling cycle = 30 + 5 + 1 = 36 minutes and in practice much sooner, since most borrowed jobs have already passed their first 30 minutes. This figure goes into the agreement between institutions and is measured in the acceptance tests.
data.sacctmgr#Accounts and QOS (sacctmgr): # Institutions: shares expressed in owned GPUs sacctmgr add account instA Description="Institution A" Fairshare=26 sacctmgr add account instB Description="Institution B" Fairshare=6 sacctmgr add account svc_llm Description="Inference service" Fairshare=1 Parent=root # Teams (example) under each institution sacctmgr add account a_physics Parent=instA Fairshare=60 sacctmgr add account a_biology Parent=instA Fairshare=40 sacctmgr add account b_lab Parent=instB Fairshare=parent # QOS sacctmgr add qos borrow sacctmgr modify qos borrow set Priority=0 PreemptMode=REQUEUE GraceTime=300 sacctmgr add qos instA sacctmgr modify qos instA set Priority=100 GrpTRES=gres/gpu=13 \ Preempt=borrow Flags=DenyOnLimit sacctmgr add qos instB sacctmgr modify qos instB set Priority=100 GrpTRES=gres/gpu=3 \ Preempt=borrow Flags=DenyOnLimit sacctmgr add qos service sacctmgr modify qos service set Priority=1000 GrpTRES=gres/gpu=16 Preempt=borrow # Attachment: owner QOS by default + the right to borrow sacctmgr modify account instA set QOS=instA,borrow DefaultQOS=instA sacctmgr modify account instB set QOS=instB,borrow DefaultQOS=instB sacctmgr modify account svc_llm set QOS=service DefaultQOS=service # Users sacctmgr add user alice Account=a_physics sacctmgr add user bob Account=b_lab Fairshare=parent on an account attaches its children to the parent for the computation [8]: B, which has a single laboratory, adds no useless level. DenyOnLimit rejects at submission a job that alone would exceed the QOS limits [8]. An 8-GPU job submitted in instB is refused immediately instead of waiting forever; the user is invited to use borrow. svc_llm receives a symbolic share: its guarantee comes from the service QOS, not from fair-share. Its consumption is re-charged to the institutions (see accounting).
data.slurm#Slurm: Slurm carries the batch workload and the guarantee. Reference numbers are [n] entries of the bibliography.
data.slurm-conf#slurm.conf (excerpts):
ClusterName=b300 SelectType=select/cons_tres SelectTypeParameters=CR_Core_Memory GresTypes=gpu NodeName=gpu[01-04] Gres=gpu:b300:8 CPUs= RealMemory= State=UNKNOWN PartitionName=gpu Nodes=gpu[01-04] Default=YES MaxTime=3-00:00:00 State=UP \ TRESBillingWeights="CPU=0.0625,Mem=0.0026G,GRES/gpu=1.0" # Accounting and enforcement of limits AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd AccountingStorageTRES=gres/gpu,gres/gpu:b300 AccountingStorageEnforce=associations,limits,qos,safe # Priority PriorityType=priority/multifactor PriorityFlags=MAX_TRES PriorityDecayHalfLife=14-0 PriorityCalcPeriod=5 PriorityMaxAge=7-0 PriorityWeightFairshare=100000 PriorityWeightQOS=20000 PriorityWeightAge=5000 PriorityWeightJobSize=0 PriorityWeightPartition=0 # Preemption PreemptType=preempt/qos PreemptMode=REQUEUE PreemptExemptTime=00:30:00 JobRequeue=1 # Isolation ProctrackType=proctrack/cgroup TaskPlugin=task/cgroup,task/affinity Reading notes:
select/cons_tres is required for sharing GRES (MPS, shard) [5] and for the preemption of heterogeneous jobs [3]. AccountingStorageTRES: declare gres/gpu and its typed variant, as the documentation recommends [6]. Declaring gres/gpu also enables gres/gpumem and gres/gpuutil [6]. AccountingStorageEnforce=...,safe: a job starts only if it can finish within its limits in TRES-minutes [4]. The fair-share weight dominates (100,000); the QOS weight (20,000) breaks ties; age (5,000) prevents starvation of an old job.
data.split#Splitting between batch and infere:
The inference service is a common good: its GPUs are taken from each share in proportion to ownership. With an inference pool of 16 GPUs (2 servers, 2 TP=8 instances):
Total share of which inference (pro rata) Guaranteed batch A 26 13 G_A = 13 B 6 3 G_B = 3 Service – – G_S = 16 With a pool of 8 GPUs the pro rata gives 6.5 and 1.5, so it is rounded to G_A = 19 and G_B = 5: fair-share, which counts continuously, rebalances the half GPU over time. The inference pool can change size with the time of day (elastic pool); the GPUs released go to borrow jobs.
data.the-qos#The QOS: QOS Cap Role instA GrpTRES=gres/gpu=G_A A’s share, never preempted instB GrpTRES=gres/gpu=G_B B’s share, never preempted service GrpTRES=gres/gpu=G_S shared vLLM instances, never preempted borrow none surplus; preemptible by the three QOS above; ordered by fair-share GrpTRES limits the total TRES allocated to all running jobs of the QOS [4]. Since G_A + G_B + G_S = 32, the sum of the guaranteed shares never exceeds the cluster. The GPUs an owner does not occupy are either free or held by borrow jobs, therefore recoverable by preemption.
data.user-side#User side: # Within one's guaranteed share (default QOS) sbatch -A a_physics --gres=gpu:b300:4 train.sh # Beyond one's share: borrowing, preemptible, must be able to resume sbatch -A a_physics --qos=borrow --requeue --gres=gpu:b300:8 \ --signal=B:TERM@300 train_checkpoint.sh The script of a borrow job traps SIGTERM, writes a checkpoint within the 300 s of GraceTime, and restarts from the last checkpoint when requeued.
data.weekly-reservation#B’s big jobs: a weekl:
B’s guaranteed share (G_B = 3 or 5) is below 8. Without a special measure, B can run a job on a whole server (TP=8, multi-GPU training) only in the borrow QOS, hence with no guaranteed delay. B is given a recurring reservation of one whole server.
# A 48 h window every week, starting Monday 8:00, for institution B scontrol create reservation ReservationName=instB_weekly \ StartTime=2026-11-02T08:00:00 Duration=2-00:00:00 Flags=WEEKLY \ Accounts=instB PartitionName=gpu NodeCnt=1 # On B's side, during the window sbatch -A b_lab --reservation=instB_weekly --qos=borrow \ --gres=gpu:b300:8 --time=2-00:00:00 training.sh Slurm’s behaviour, from the reservation documentation [21]:
WEEKLY makes the reservation recurring: it activates and deactivates itself every week. During the window, the reserved resources serve only the reservation’s jobs: “no other jobs can use those resources”. Unused reserved time is charged to the reservation’s users or accounts, in equal parts. Here all of it goes to instB. B therefore pays for its window in fair-share whether it uses it or not. That is fair (the server was taken from the others) and it encourages reserving only what will be used. B submits in the borrow QOS, not in instB whose 3-GPU cap would block an 8-GPU job. The preemption risk is nil: no owner job of A can enter the reserved server. Sizing. B’s weekly share is 6 x 168 = 1,008 GPU-hours. A 48 h window costs 8 x 48 = 384 GPU-hours, 38 % of its share. The rest is consumed in instB and borrow. The agreement fixes the duration; a 126 h window would exhaust all of B’s share in a whole server.
Before each window, Slurm must start on the chosen server only jobs that finish before it opens. borrow jobs that declare a short --time then keep filling that server until the last minute. This behaviour is verified in the acceptance tests (test 9). For B, the job must also fit the window: --time less than or equal to the remaining duration.

data.claude-code#Code assistant: Claude Code:
Claude Code can also talk to the gateway, through ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, with the virtual key as the credential. The full, sourced instructions are on the Coding agents page; the short version:
Models. Anthropic does not support routing Claude Code to non-Claude models through any gateway, so Claude Code against the local vLLM models of this cluster is possible but unsupported by Anthropic. The supported path is Claude models through the gateway’s opt-in anthropic provider (gateway v0.12.0), billed to the organisation’s API account. Pooling Pro or Max subscriptions is not allowed. Continue accepts any OpenAI-compatible provider, LiteLLM and vLLM included: provider: openai with a custom apiBase [16]. The configuration file (~/.continue/config.yaml on macOS and Linux, %USERPROFILE%\.continue\config.yaml on Windows; Continue configuration) requires the fields name, version and schema. Each model declares roles among chat, autocomplete, embed, rerank, edit, apply and summarize [17].

It is referenced as a secret (${{ secrets.... }} [17]), never written in clear in a versioned file. Autocompletion sends a request on every keystroke. Serve it with a small dedicated model (an instance of a few GPUs, or MIG) and set an rpm_limit on the key, or it will eat the institution’s quota. contextLength must not exceed the vLLM instance’s --max-model-len.
data.remote-ssh#Development and jobs: Remote-:
Remote-SSH reads the user’s ~/.ssh/config [18]. Target the login node, never a GPU node: GPU nodes are reached only through a Slurm job, otherwise the work escapes fair-share and cgroup isolation.
# ~/.ssh/config Host b300-bastion HostName bastion.example.org User alice IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_b300 Host b300-login HostName login.b300.internal User alice IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_b300 ProxyJump b300-bastion // settings.json (VS Code, user) { "remote.SSH.remotePlatform": { "b300-login": "linux" } } remote.SSH.remotePlatform maps a host to its platform [18]. The login node is shared by many users, so also enable Remote.SSH: Remote Server Listen On Socket in the Settings UI (the page cited names it only by that label). The VS Code server then listens on a Unix socket locked to the user instead of a forwarded TCP port. This needs a Linux or macOS host, disables connection multiplexing, and makes public-key authentication recommended (Remote Development troubleshooting).
The VS Code server consumes CPU and memory on the login node. Set per-user limits on that node (systemd cgroups) so that one session does not penalise the others. Do not run computation on the login node: go through srun/sbatch.
