data.jwt#OpenID Connect tokens on the inferen:
With a jwt block, a bearer token that has the JWS compact shape (three dot-separated segments) is verified by go-authn/oidc instead of being looked up as a virtual key. The library refuses alg: none and every HMAC algorithm (so the issuer’s public key cannot be used as an HS256 secret), compares iss whole, requires aud and exp, bounds the clock skew, and fetches keys over https only, at most once per min_refresh. type = "at+jwt" refuses ID tokens (RFC 9068). Discovery happens at start-up: a gateway whose issuer does not answer does not start.
The gateway only maps the verified identity: the map blocks are tried in order, and the first whose claim (default groups) holds value gives the team and an optional project. Each person is one synthetic key, so the limits of the block (rpm, tpm, max_inflight), budgets, IP allowlists and spend reports apply as to a key. Every refusal is the same 401; the reason is logged on the server only.
data.key-rotation#Key rotation: POST /admin/keys/{id}/rotate gives a key a new secret; the key keeps its ID, so limits, budgets, allowlists and reports continue. The replaced secret stays valid for grace_period (at most 720h), or is revoked at once if absent. PUT /admin/keys/{id}/rotation schedules it: every (1h to 8784h), grace_period and a target, a vault: reference under vault_prefix/
data.networks#Networks, proxies and secrets: trusted_proxies lists the reverse proxies whose X-Forwarded-For is believed; it is read from the right, skipping them. routes { admin | metrics | healthz | inference { allow = [...] } } restricts each route class to networks; metrics and healthz default to loopback. IP allowlists on an organisation, a team or a key (GET, PUT /admin/allowlists) must all match the client, else 403 with one generic message. Every *_file attribute is a secret reference: a path, or a field of an OpenBao or HashiCorp Vault KV v2 secret, vault:/#, which needs the vault block (https only, no redirect followed, reads cached). User names may contain @ and +. See the gateway’s limitations 11 to 14 for what this does not do yet.
data.saml#SAML federations: RENATER, eduGAIN:
A SAML federation goes through go-authn/bridge (authn-bridge), an OpenID provider in front of the federation. Register the gateway as one of its clients and point sso.issuer (and jwt.issuer) at the bridge. The bridge’s configuration is its own, documented in go-authn’s repositories; the gateway’s README gives this client block:
# authn-bridge configuration, not the gateway's client "llmflow-admin" { secret_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/llmflow-admin.secret" redirect_uris = ["https://llm.example.org/admin/callback"] id_token_claims = true # the bridge's ID tokens carry no claims about the person otherwise } Ask for scopes = ["openid", "profile", "groups"]: the bridge’s groups are entitlements held to the identity provider that asserted them, so a role block can match urn:mace:... or urn:geant:... values. (This block belongs to authn-bridge, not to llmflow-gateway, so check-config cannot check it.) See also the guide.
data.scim#SCIM provisioning:
With a scim block, an identity provider (Entra ID, Okta, Keycloak) provisions users and groups at /scim/v2 (RFC 7643, RFC 7644); the protocol is go-authn/scim, and the gateway stores what is pushed.
A provisioned user is a gateway user of the same userName (letters, digits and _ . - @ +, at most 128), disabled while active is false or after deletion, which revokes their admin tokens. The members of a mapped group get the block’s role on its team (member by default, team_admin or viewer); leaving the group, deactivation or deletion takes it away. Only those provisioned (role, team) pairs are managed: roles granted by hand stay. The state is reconciled after every change and at start-up. The bearer token is compared in constant time; /scim/v2 obeys the routes.admin networks.
data.sso#Administrator single sign-on:
With an sso block, administrators log in with OpenID Connect in a browser instead of holding an admin token (go-authn/rp: authorization code with PKCE, state, nonce, ID-token verification).
GET /admin/login redirects to the provider; GET /admin/callback ends the login and redirects to GET /admin/session, which returns the user, their roles and the session’s csrf_token. POST /admin/logout ends the session. The roles are the role blocks the person’s claims match, plus the roles of the gateway user of the same name, read from the store on every request. Somebody with neither is refused at the callback. The session is a random 256-bit value in a __Host-llmflow-session cookie (Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax), stored server-side as its SHA-256. CSRF: a state-changing request authenticated by the cookie must carry the session’s token in X-CSRF-Token and must not be cross-site (Sec-Fetch-Site) or come from another Origin than the redirect_url’s. Bearer-token requests are unaffected. Sessions live in the memory of one replica: behind several, use sticky sessions.
data.verified#OIDC verified against real iden:
The JWT path (go-authn/oidc), SSO (go-authn/rp) and SCIM had met only test keys. The e2e/oidc suite of bench v0.3.0 runs the same checks against two real providers, each behind a counting proxy that stands in as the issuer, so every key-set fetch the gateway makes is counted.
dex v2.46.1, the upstream container (the fleet’s claimward/dex is an unmodified fork 232 commits behind it, and was not used). go-authn/bridge v0.23.4 in front of a test SAML federation and identity provider written in Go; the provider’s metadata, responses and (encrypted) assertions go through xmlsec1 1.3.12. Gateway under test: v0.8.0, with two organisations, jwt and sso role mappings and a scim group binding. All checks pass for both providers:
Check Evidence (a) a token is accepted and charged to its organisation and team llmflow_requests_total and /admin/spend per team (b) wrong audience; signed by another key; alg: none; HS256 keyed with the public key (PEM and DER); expired 401 with a body identical to a garbage bearer’s (an expired token is refused after exp plus the 5 s clock skew) (b) 40 tokens with unknown kids exactly 1 key-set fetch at the provider (c) signing-key rotation the old (unexpired) and the new token both 200, 1 fetch; an SSO login right after works (d) SSO: code, PKCE S256, state, nonce __Host-llmflow-session cookie (Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax); role org_admin in /admin/whoami (d) replayed callback; callback in another browser; no role binding; logout 400; 400; 403; logout without the CSRF token 403, with it 200, then the old cookie 401 (e) an org_admin of organisation A against organisation B 13 admin listings without leaks; 6 writes on B answer 403 (control: the same write on A answers 200); 7 UI pages without B (f) SCIM user and group to role team_admin visible in /admin/users/.../roles and in the person’s session Findings (the first two were fixed in gateway v0.10.0; the third was still open when this was written):
gateway #60: SSO’s ID-token key set refreshed at most once a minute (a fixed default), so a provider rotation right after start-up refused logins; observed with dex rotating every 30 s. Fixed: sso.min_refresh (default 1 minute, at least 5 s, as for jwt); lower it for a provider that rotates faster. gateway #61: the README said keys are fetched over https only, but http to a loopback issuer is accepted. Fixed in the README: it now states this as go-authn/oidc’s deliberate exemption (a loopback connection crosses no network link). Read “https only” above as “https, except loopback”. go-authn/bridge #79: the signing-key rotation procedure is not documented in the bridge’s README; the one the test used (authn-bridge keygen, retired_signing_key_files, then a restart) works.

data.api#Using it: s := pii.New() // every kind; pii.New(pii.IBAN, pii.Card) for some ms := s.Find(text) // []pii.Match{Kind, Start, End}, ordered, no overlap clean := pii.Mask(text, ms, pii.Placeholder) // "IBAN [IBAN], mail [EMAIL]" pii.MaxLen (254 bytes) bounds the length of any match. A caller masking a stream can hold back the last MaxLen bytes, and will then never release the start of a match whose end it has not seen yet.
data.false-positives#False positives, measure:
testdata/benign.txt contains no personal data by construction: 45 lines of text a model reads and writes every day (versions, OIDs, dates, UUIDs, hashes, ISBN, EAN, SIREN and SIRET numbers, prices, MAC addresses, C++ and Rust ::, an SSH git remote, and a card number, a NIR and an IBAN with wrong keys). TestFalsePositives fails if a count rises above what was measured.
iban, nir, card, email, ipv4, ipv6: 0 false positives. phone: 1, ref 0123456789, a valid French number in every respect except its meaning. Phone numbers are the one kind that cannot be checked. A guardrail that masks them will also mask 10-digit references starting with 0.
data.pii#pii:
Finds personal data in text, in pure Go with no dependencies (standard library only, CGO_ENABLED=0). It was written for the PII guardrail of the gateway, which masks prompts before they reach the model and masks completions before they reach the client. The package itself only reports what it found and where; the caller decides what to do with it. Repository →
This page is written from the repository’s README at v0.1.0. v0.1.0 is quadratic on long runs of digits and should be upgraded to v0.2.0 or later: see Security. The README of v0.2.0 also compares pii with Microsoft Presidio; this page has not been rewritten from it.
go get github.com/go-llmflow/pii@v0.1.0
data.recognisers#What a match means:
A recogniser that has a check digit uses it. A match is therefore a value that could exist, not just a string with the right number of digits.
Kind Recognised by Checked by iban 2 letters, 2 digits, then alphanumerics; single spaces allowed ISO 13616: the exact length for the country, and mod 97 = 1 nir the French social security number: sex 1/2/3/4/7/8, year, month, department (2A/2B for Corsica), commune, order number, 2-digit key key = 97 - (the 13 digits mod 97), with 2A read as 19 and 2B as 18 (INSEE) card 13 to 19 digits, single spaces or dashes allowed Luhn (ISO/IEC 7812-1 annex B), plus a known network’s prefix and length: Visa, Mastercard, American Express, Discover, JCB, Diners email a practical subset of RFC 5322 addr-spec local part at most 64 octets and address at most 254 (RFC 5321). A git@host:path remote is not treated as a mailbox phone E.164 (+, at most 15 digits) and the French plan (0 + 9 digits, +33 / 0033) format only, since phone numbers have no checksum ipv4 dotted decimal, not inside a longer dotted run (version numbers, OIDs) net/netip ipv6 the three text forms of RFC 4291, including a trailing IPv4 net/netip; zones are not accepted When two candidates overlap, the one that starts first wins, then the longer one, then the checksum-validated kind.
data.security#Security and performance:
The input is untrusted (prompts and model output). Every regular expression runs on Go’s RE2 engine, in linear time. FuzzFind checks that matches are ordered and within bounds, that every checksum-validated match re-validates on its own, and that masking twice gives the same result as masking once. The tests also run with GOARCH=386.
BenchmarkFind scans 64 KiB of the benign corpus. The comparison against Microsoft Presidio, the reference in this domain, has not been made yet.

data.a9#The pii defect (A9):
Its own README, at v0.2.0, says what was measured: 1 MiB of 1 1 1 ... took 11 min 56 s with v0.1.0 (measured 2026-10-26, on a loaded machine). Since v0.2.0 card candidates are bounded at 19 digits, patterns of bounded length are searched in 512-byte windows, and TestLongRunsStayLinear checks the growth from 128 KiB to 2 MiB on twelve adversarial inputs (linear is x16, and the test fails above x64). The gateway’s README gives the same defect as 5 to 20 minutes; the two figures were measured separately. Upgrade pii to v0.2.0 or later.
The hide_secrets guardrail uses gitsafe’s redact. Its README at v0.17.1 says that since that version it finds the issuers’ prefixes with strings.Index instead of stepping a regular-expression automaton through the whole text: identical results (compared on 20,000 generated texts and by a fuzz target), and about 30 times faster on the gateway’s 2 KB benchmark prompt, 4 us instead of 130 us on an Apple M4 Max on 2026-10-26, measured on a loaded machine, so only an order of magnitude.
data.chaos#Chaos results:
PostgreSQL ran behind a fault-injecting proxy (the README names a real PostgreSQL) that could refuse connections or blackhole them.
Fault Behaviour PostgreSQL down An unknown key gets 503, not 401, and is not cached as invalid. A cached key is served until the budgets are 3 refresh periods old, then everything fails closed; everything recovers. PostgreSQL partitioned 503 within 5 s; fail-closed on time; recovery when the partition heals. PostgreSQL restarted A call that draws a dead pooled connection fails safe with a 503 (one call in the test); the pool recovers by itself. Accounting during an outage With v0.9.0, every record of the requests served during the outage was lost (21 of 21 in the test, 2026-10-26). With v0.10.0’s durable spool, 21 of 21 are stored once, with 21 distinct ids. Two replicas, one database A concurrent first start works; keys are shared; a revocation reaches the other replica after key_cache_ttl; the audit chain stays one verifiable chain under two concurrent writers. Upstream killed mid-stream, restarted The client gets the partial stream; counters return to zero; the next requests are served. Key rotated with 16 requests in flight All 16 finish and are charged to the key; the old secret is refused at once and the new one is served. Clock stepped back 2 h The audit chain still verifies. Export target down The queue drops beyond 256 MiB and alerts. Clients that stop reading Released after max_request_duration + 5 s. The accounting loss is fixed in v0.10.0. Every batch of usage records is appended to a spool file and fsync’d before it is inserted into PostgreSQL, and a record is stored at most once (its id is the request id). From the README of v0.10.0, measured on 2026-10-26: TestChaosAccountingOutage stores 21 of 21 records after a PostgreSQL outage, where v0.9.0 lost all 21; with the real binary, 20 records were spooled while PostgreSQL was unreachable, the gateway was killed with SIGKILL and restarted, and 21 of 21 records were stored, with 21 distinct ids and no double billing. This is not a promise of zero loss: a record still in the in-memory queue when the process dies (about the last second of traffic) is lost, and past spool_max_bytes (256 MiB per process by default) a batch the store refuses is lost too, counted in llmflow_accounting_failed_total and alerted as accounting_records_lost. store.spool_dir is mandatory with the postgres store since v0.10.0; see Upgrading to v0.10.0.
data.dependencies#Dependencies: govulncheck (database of 2026-10-21) finds nothing in the gateway built with Go 1.27.3. go-authn/oidc v0.4.2, go-authn/rp v0.1.2 and go-volumes/s3 v0.2.0 declare go 1.27.1: built with that toolchain, nine standard-library vulnerabilities are reachable from them (net/http, crypto/tls, crypto/x509; fixed in Go 1.27.2 and 1.27.3). The gateway’s binary is not affected because it is built with 1.27.3, but those modules should raise their go line. go-authn/scim v0.1.0 is clean. The gateway v0.10.0 takes the new releases at the go 1.27.3 floor: oidc v0.4.3, rp v0.2.0, scim v0.1.1, s3 v0.2.1, pii v0.2.1.
data.findings#Findings: ID Severity Finding Fix A1 medium Multimodal uuids were scoped per tenant on chat and Responses only. On rerank, tokenize and embeddings the client’s uuid reached vLLM unchanged: one tenant could probe or poison another’s cached media. scoped on all routes, still reusable within a tenant (#48, #55) A2 medium A client that never read its answer blocked its handler for ever, holding up to 64 MiB of buffered answer, its key’s in-flight slot and its fair-share grant. A few connections could exhaust the gateway’s memory. every response has a write deadline of max_request_duration + 5 s (#49) A3 high Any organisation admin could re-enable a user a proxy admin had disabled, with every role the user kept, proxy_admin included (POST /admin/users on an existing name). POST /admin/users on a disabled user answers 403 unless the caller is a proxy admin (#50) A4 low A key created while its team was being disabled stayed valid, and disabling a team did not clear the cache of verified JWTs. disabling an organisation, team or project cuts its keys and cached JWTs at once (#51) A5 medium Export queues were bounded in objects only: with S3 down and content logging on, up to 8 GiB of request logs could pile up in memory. queues capped at 256 MiB; beyond that, objects are dropped, counted and alerted (#52) A6 medium Store calls were unbounded: during a partition with PostgreSQL, requests with an uncached key hung (no answer after 20 s in the test), and a stuck budget refresh stopped every later one. key lookups give up after 5 s (503), a budget refresh after 30 s, admin, UI and SCIM after 60 s (#54) A7 low Two replicas started together on an empty database raced on the schema, and one failed to start. schema creation is serialised (#54) A8 low The admin API, SSO and SCIM answers had no nosniff, CSP or frame denial (the UI had them). those answers carry nosniff, a CSP and no-store (#56) A9 high go-llmflow/pii v0.1.0, used by the pii guardrail, is quadratic on long runs of digits: any key holder of a guarded team could pin a core per request. fixed in pii v0.2.0, bumped in the gateway (#57) Each fix has a test that fails without it. A3 is the only one that crosses organisations; the matrix found no other cross-organisation hole on the 39 admin routes.
data.method#Method: Read, then attack. The threat model and the code were read first. vLLM’s own sources were opened wherever the gateway relies on how vLLM parses a request (vllm-project/vllm main at 256d8b4: the scoring, embedding and Anthropic protocol files). Scope. Every package of the module, and the modules it pulls for authentication and storage: go-authn/oidc v0.4.2, go-authn/rp v0.1.2, go-authn/scim v0.1.0 and go-volumes/s3 v0.2.0. The fixes of earlier reviews were rechecked and hold, with their tests. A route by role matrix. TestAuthzMatrix calls every admin route of the router (a route without a row fails the test) as 12 principals on one organisation’s objects: the master key, proxy_admin, proxy_viewer, the org_admin of the organisation and of another one (the cross-organisation attacker), team_admin, member, a team viewer and an organisation viewer, a user without roles, an inference key, and a JWT-shaped bearer. Listings are checked for leaks to outsiders, and the matrix was checked against planted mistakes. Fuzzing. The 29 existing targets ran for 10 minutes each on v0.8.0, three at a time with two workers each: none failed, and no new crasher was found. A new target, FuzzScopeEveryRoute, ran for 60 s with no failure; it caught a planted regression on its first seed and is part of the CI fuzz smoke. govulncheck (vulnerability database of 2026-10-21) on the module and on the four modules above.
data.residual#Residual risks: Usage served during a store outage is not recorded fixed in v0.10.0 (see above). What remains is the last second of in-memory queue on a crash, and a full spool. SCIM adopts an existing gateway user with the same userName, and re-enables it if a proxy admin had disabled it by hand. The identity provider is already trusted for usernames through SSO. Roles that SSO maps from ID-token claims are fixed at login, for the session’s lifetime. Stored roles and the disabled flag are read on every request. A member may point their own key’s scheduled rotation at any field under the team’s Vault prefix, overwriting a secret delivered there for another key of the team: a denial of service inside the team, with no read access. Secret files are read whatever their permissions (Kubernetes mounts secrets 0644 by default). Keep them in a directory only the gateway’s user can read. A tool server’s error message (at most 4 KiB) is returned to the MCP client: tool servers are configured, so they are trusted. The gateway’s limitations list the open defects, re-checked in this audit.
data.security#Security: On 2026-10-26 an independent, adversarial review of gateway v0.8.0 (commit b23064a) was made by an agent that did not write the code, together with chaos tests on the parts that keep state. Its fixes are released in v0.9.0. This page summarises it; the gateway’s README, section “Security audit 2026-10-26”, at the v0.9.0 tag is the source, and where the two differ the README wins.
data.verified#Verified without a finding:
No cross-organisation IDOR on the 39 admin routes; CSRF protection (synchronizer token, Origin, Sec-Fetch-Site) on every state change of the UI and of cookie-authenticated API calls; a fresh session at login, __Host- cookies, no open redirect; every outbound URL comes from the configuration and no client redirect is followed; keys, tokens and the master key compared in constant time over hashes and never logged; a fallback keeps the original organisation’s cache salt, uuids and priority; scheduled-rotation targets stay under their team’s Vault prefix; export keys validated against traversal; request bodies read only after authentication and bounded.
Against a real vLLM, the end-to-end run of bench v0.2.0 (2026-10-26) confirmed that a client’s priority, vllm_xargs, extra_body and cache_salt change neither the scheduling order nor the cache isolation, and that prefix-cache isolation per organisation holds: vLLM’s own counters showed 768 of 814 prefix tokens hit within one organisation and 0 of 814 from another.
